10483-short-stories-old-and-new:
C. Alphonso Smith, Poe Professor of English at the University of Virginia, selected and edited this 1916 anthology of short stories old and new. Smith, author of a study of the American short story, chose classics that show the form's range, from Bible and Arabian Nights to modern masters. The book serves students and general readers alike.

Esther, Ali Baba, Rip Van Winkle, The Gold-Bug, A Christmas Carol, and The Gift of the Magi stand beside Hawthorne, Maupassant, Kipling, and Stevenson. Each tale is a model of plot, character, or surprise. Readers get a strong, readable survey of the short story at its best.
11033-the-angel-over-the-right-shoulder-:
An 1852 New Year tale by the author of Sunny Side, this short book follows Mrs. James, a busy mother who feels her work is never done. A lamp that will not burn starts a talk with her husband, who teases that she only needs system. Mrs. James answers that he should follow her for one day and see what she must do, without an uninterrupted half hour from morning to night.

Her husband proposes an experiment: two hours each day set apart for her own private use, locked in her room, letting other work wait. Mrs. James doubts any man knows a woman's work, yet she promises to try. The tale, gentle and domestic, argues for rest, order, and respect for household labour at the start of a new year.
1107-the-taming-of-the-shrew:
In Padua, the sharp-tongued Katharina scares off every suitor, which blocks her sweet sister Bianca's marriage. Enter Petruchio, a fortune-hunting gentleman who weds Kate and sets out to "tame" her with wit, hunger, and sleepless nights. William Shakespeare's early comedy plays the battle of the sexes for laughs.

The war of words is fast and rude, and the play within a play that frames it adds a further joke. Modern readers debate its harshness, and modern stages play it many ways. The comedy's verve and its famous speeches keep it on stage, quarrels and all.
11464-cuba-old-and-new:
Albert G Robinson's 1915 book moves between Cuba under Spain and Cuba after independence. Early chapters walk the country, old Havana, and new Havana in turn. Then the reader is carried around the island town by town, with pictures of streets, harbours, and country roads.

Later chapters take up the United States and Cuba, the island's revolts, and filibustering. Sugar, other crops, and various products and industries follow. Politics, government, and commerce close the account. Photographs show the flag raising of May 1902 and a planter's home, giving the history a visible, human scale.
11608-from-a-girl-s-point-of-view:
Lilian Bell's 1897 essays, From a Girl's Point of View, open with the untrained man under thirty-five and the philosophy of clothes. Woman's rights in love, men as lovers, love-making as a fine art, and girls and other girls follow.

Bell writes with a sharp, teasing voice, warning that critics of girls who say I don't think should take care, since most girls, she jokes, don't think at all. Age, she adds, has little to do with it, and thirty-five is only an approximate figure for a man's ripeness. The book is a witty American woman's view of courtship and manners.
13760-john-rutherford-the-white-chief-a-:
James Drummond edited this account of John Rutherford, an English sailor who lived among the Maori in New Zealand. Rutherford, shipwrecked or captured in the 1820s, became a chief among his hosts. A drawing made in 1828 fronts the volume, with pictures of mats, clubs, and Kororareka Beach. Drummond presents the tale as adventure, with notes on Maori life.

Tribes flocked to ports to trade for iron tools and guns when Europeans arrived. Rutherford's story shows tattooing, warfare, and daily custom from the inside. Modern readers should note that parts of the tale are disputed by historians. Still, the book captures early contact between Maori and Europeans. It remains a vivid, if debated, travel narrative.
14462-the-third-and-last-part-of-conny-c:
R. G., probably Robert Greene, published this third part of Conny-catching in 1592, exposing the tricks of London sharpers and adding the new art of fool-taking. The title page promises villainies never before discovered.

A woman decoy lures a gentleman with flattery and a purse, while confederates pick his pocket and vanish. Other chapters catalogue card cheats, false beggars, and cutpurses at work in London. The pamphlet mixes warning with entertainment. It is a vivid rogue's guide to Elizabethan street crime, written in the slang of its day. Readers then bought such pamphlets as warnings and entertainment.
1508-the-taming-of-the-shrew:
Shakespeare's Paduan comedy opens with a drunken tinker, Christopher Sly, tricked into believing he is a lord watching a play. The play within tells of Petruchio, who weds the sharp-tongued Katherina and sets out to tame her, while her sister Bianca is courted by a crowd of suitors in disguise.

Through wordplay, trickery, and a famous wager on wifely obedience, the comedy tests who rules a marriage and who only seems to. Modern readers debate its ending, but its wit still sparkles. It remains one of Shakespeare's liveliest, most argued-over comedies.
15225-andreas-the-legend-of-st-andrew:
Robert Kilburn Root translated Andreas, the Old English legend of St. Andrew, for Yale Studies in English in 1899. His introduction weighs authorship, noting that early editors gave the poem to Cynewulf for its style, while Fritsche and Sievers doubted the link. Trautman later backed the older view.

The poem itself tells Andrew's missionary adventures in a heroic, alliterative style, with sea voyages, captivity, and miracles. Root's translation keeps the story clear for modern readers while notes track the scholarly debate. Students of medieval poetry will find the volume a solid, readable entry to a fine old poem.
15465-parisian-points-of-view:
Ludovic Halévy's short stories, translated by Edith V. B. Matthews with an introduction by Brander Matthews, were published by Harper in 1894. The American introduction notes that Halévy was best known in the United States for The Abbé Constantin, a gentle French novel that pleased readers tired of Zola's morals and Ohnet's taste. These tales offer a different, sharper Paris.

Nine stories follow: Only a Waltz, The Dancing-Master, The Circus Charger, Blacky, The Most Beautiful Woman in Paris, The Story of a Ball-Dress, The Insurgent, The Chinese Ambassador, and In the Express. Balls, circuses, trains, and drawing rooms give each tale its stage. Halévy writes with light irony and a Frenchman's eye for manners, and the set works as a pleasant entry to French short fiction of the period.
15586-india-old-and-new:
Sir Valentine Chirol, author of Indian Unrest and The Egyptian Problem, published this study of India in London in 1921, with Macmillan. An epigraph quotes Sir Thomas Munro of Madras in 1824, hoping Indian subjects might in time govern and protect themselves. Sixteen chapters run from the clash of two civilisations to the Indian problem as a world problem.

Chapters trace Hinduism's enduring power, Mahomedan domination, British rule under the East India Company, and the Mutiny and fifty years after. Unrest, the Morley-Minto reforms, the Great War, and the great Indian reform bill follow. Gandhi emerges, elections and cross currents in southern India are weighed, and an Indian parliament is born. Chirol writes as a British observer at the reform moment, sympathetic to self-rule yet wary of the road ahead.
1596-smoke-bellew:
Jack London's Smoke Bellew follows Christopher Bellew, called Chris at college, Kit in San Francisco's Bohemian crowd, and Smoke in the Klondike. The taste of meat, a stampede to Squaw Creek, and a race for Number One test a city man against the North. Shorty Dreams and the man on the other bank join the adventures.

The tales are strung as a single growth: a soft young man hardens into a Yukon traveller, learning hunger, cold, and the code of the trail. London writes with vigour and humour. Smoke Bellew is a classic Klondike book, and a fine introduction to London's Northland tales.
16615-by-still-waters-lyrical-poems-old-:
A. E. put out this 1906 book of short lyric poems through the Dun Emer Press at Dundrum. Old and new pieces sit side by side, from a prelude and songs of night, dawn, and day to poems on memory, parting, prayer, heroes, and the soul. Ten pieces came from an early song book and others from later verse books.

The poems are brief, musical, and full of light, dusk, wind, and inner quiet. They turn on faith, loss, and the hope of a life beyond sight, in plain yet lofty words. Readers who like short, song-like verse will find much here to read aloud and sit with, piece by piece, rather than in one rush.
16616-the-nuts-of-knowledge-lyrical-poem:
A. E. gathers lyrical poems old and new in this Dun Emer Press volume, dedicated to Brian when he is grown up. The Nuts of Knowledge, Immortality, The Hermit, The Great Breath, and The Divine Vision lead the contents. Aphrodite, Krishna, A Call of the Sidhe, and The Grey Eros stand among the later pieces. Ten poems each come from Homeward Songs and The Earth Breath.

A. E. writes in a mystical Irish mode, full of twilight trees, secret streams, and visions of beauty. The book is short and songlike, meant to be read slowly. Readers of Irish poetry will find a compact, haunting collection from a poet-painter of the Celtic revival.
16742-dan-merrithew:
Lawrence Perry wrote this 1910 sea tale of a young tug man, issued by A. L. Burt in New York with color plates. Dan works the tug Hydrographer near Norfolk. He meets a girl on the yacht Veiled Ladye. Then he is drawn into fights, a lost boat, and a party. Machine guns, an attack, a burning ship, and a night on a wreck follow. Fifteen chapters carry him from first meeting to close.

Perry mixes sea work, daring rescues, and young love with brisk, plain action. Dan stakes his life more than once, and his courage wins the girl and the day. The tale is old-style adventure for boys and for all who like ships, storms, and a hero who keeps his nerve when the worst hits.
19036-germany-and-the-germans-from-an-am:
Price Collier wrote this 1913 survey of Germany and the Germans from an American point of view. He traces the cradle of modern Germany from Frederick the Great to Bismarck, then turns to parties, press, Berlin, professors, women, the army, and German problems. The book appeared just before the First World War.

Collier follows tribes along the Rhine and Danube, noting how rivers divided North from South in speech and custom, and how Suevi customs kept men from growing rich on fixed land. His tone is frank and curious. Readers get a pre-war American portrait of a rising power, its strengths and its strains.
19489-canoe-mates-in-canada-or-three-boy:
St. George Rathborne wrote this boys' adventure of three lads afloat on the Saskatchewan River, published in Chicago in the early nineteen teens. Paddling canoes through whirlpools, camping by firelight, and cooking meat and vegetables on a spit over open flame fill their days.

One scene has a boy paddling hard to escape being sucked into the largest whirlpool on their course. The book belongs to a series on woodcraft and water life, and it teaches camp skills through action rather than lecture, which is why boys kept it on their shelves.
20242-left-on-labrador-or-the-cruise-of-:
C. A. Stephens wrote Left on Labrador, on the cruise of the schooner-yacht Curlew. Stephens addresses readers of Camping Out, the first Camping-Out Series volume. They will recall the graphite lode found by the young party there. Raed was left to dispose of that find as he saw fit.

The season was too advanced for a trip to Katahdin that fall. So the whole affair waited till the following spring came round. Stephens mixes New England camping with a Labrador cruise in one tale. Readers get outdoor adventure from a master of boys' wilderness stories.
2042-something-new:
P. G. Wodehouse opens a comic novel on a bright London morning, where a young man steps out of a quiet side street into a city full of schemes. Ashe Marson, a writer of adventure tales, soon finds work that is stranger than his fiction. Wodehouse wrote Something New in 1915, as his comic voice was taking its famous light shape.

A theft, a country house, and a cast of servants, crooks, and hopeful lovers tangle the plot, while Wodehouse keeps the tone light and the dialogue sharp. The book shows his early gift for farce, long before Blandings and Jeeves became household names. The country-house theft plot lets him mix servants, lovers, and crooks without ever losing the joke.
20743-the-marx-he-knew:
John Spargo, an American socialist writer, published The Marx He Knew in 1909. Old Hans speaks with deep respect of the man in a portrait on the wall. A young comrade listens while a clock ticks through a long, tense silence.

Spargo frames Karl Marx through the voice of one who knew him. The tale form lets big ideas arrive as memory and talk. Readers get a warm, human Marx rather than a dry life story. The book also shows how early American socialists spread Marx's name through story as much as through theory.
21696-red-rooney-the-last-of-the-crew:
R. M. Ballantyne strands a sailor in Greenland in Red Rooney, the last of his crew. The tale is set at the end of the eighteenth century, near Baffin's Bay. Nature there seems to keep a workshop for the making of icebergs.

A solitary man staggers over the frozen sea, his will strong and his powers nearly spent. His sealskin garb looks native, but his brown locks and bushy beard betray a stranger. Polar bears, seals, and Greenland whales share his world of ice. Ballantyne builds a tale of Inuit life and one castaway's faint, clutching hope of shelter.
2245-the-taming-of-the-shrew:
Petruchio arrives in Padua determined to wed the sharp-tongued Katharina, whose temper has scared off every suitor. The Taming of the Shrew follows his campaign of paradox and patience, starving, scolding, and praising her into submission, while her younger sister Bianca collects rivals of her own. Shakespeare frames the tale as a play performed for a drunken tinker.

The comedy's treatment of marriage has provoked argument for centuries, and modern stagings often play Katharina's final speech with irony. Its energy, wordplay, and farcical subplots keep it fiercely alive on stage. Readers will find a play that entertains and unsettles in the same breath.
22895-the-point-of-view:
Van Manderpootz, a great man of modest habits, presides over The Point of View. For all his eminence, van Manderpootz shrinks from notice like the shyest flower in the garden, or so the narrator swears. At that point the speaker pauses, and his broad red face tries hard to look violet-like. The comedy is built into the description.

Stories in this vein mix laboratory wonders with social farce. A point of view, in such tales, is rarely just a camera angle. It is a machine, a drug, or a trick that lets one mind sample another's outlook. The excerpt promises wit more than dread. Readers get a light, clever piece of early science fiction, carried by its narrator's cheerful unreliability.
22902-the-liberty-boys-running-the-block:
Harry Moore sets The Liberty Boys Running the Blockade in Revolutionary New York. Turning into Broad Street, the boys walk down at once, and a possible spy takes the same direction. At Broad and Pearl stood Fraunces Tavern, a favorite haunt of officers and fashionable men, and so a natural hangout for the boys.

The Liberty Boys were the heroes of a long dime-novel series, young patriots forever foiling British plots. Getting out of New York, the subtitle promises, will take nerve and luck. Spies, blockades, and tavern talk supply the action. The history is costume, worn lightly. Readers meet popular fiction built for boys of a later century, still galloping.
24933-the-man-who-knew:
Edgar Wallace published The Man Who Knew in Boston in 1918, with a frontispiece by William A. Kirkpatrick. John Minute, a rich man with a laboratory at Weald Lodge, finds himself swindled by a man called Rex Holland, whom nobody but Frank Merrill claims to have seen. Detective Inspector Nash of Scotland Yard takes up the case.

Chapters follow an accountant at a bank, John Minute's legacy, a murder, and the trial of Frank Merrill, who stands accused while a double walks free. A letter in the grate and a man who came to Montreux turn the plot. Wallace writes with brisk pace and sharp twists, in one of his best-known crime novels.
25692-an-epitome-of-the-homeopathic-heal:
B. L. Hill, professor of anatomy and late professor of surgery, obstetrics, and diseases of females and children, writes this 1859 epitome of the homoeopathic healing art, published in Cleveland and Chicago. It holds new discoveries and improvements to the present time.

Hill designs the book for families, for travellers on their journey, and as a pocket companion for physicians. A table of remedies, with figures affixed to each remedy, opens the practical section, guiding readers to homoeopathic treatments for common complaints in a compact, portable form. Hill also wrote a homoeopathic practice of surgery.
26218-the-young-oarsmen-of-lakeview:
Captain Ralph Bonehill's boys' book follows Jerry, Harry, and Blumpo through rowing races and lakeside scrapes. Contents list a runaway horse at Mrs. Fleming's, Jerry's bravery, the saving of a sloop, and a single shell race. Later chapters bring tar and feathers, a trip to Hermit Island, an attack in the dark, and the hermit's secret.

A hotel robbery, a red valise, a yacht mishap, and a villain named Alexander Slocum drive the later plot. Nellie Ardell's troubles, a tramp, and a crazy man's doings add danger and comedy. The book closes with a last race and good-bye to the rival oarsmen, praising pluck, teamwork, and fair play on the water.
26369-amy-harrison-or-heavenly-seed-and-:
This short moral tale for children follows two sisters, Amy and Kitty Harrison, who walk half a mile from their mother's cottage to Sunday school in a nearby village. Their teacher is Mrs. Mordaunt, the clergyman's wife, who sometimes draws a lesson from the wild flowers the girls gather by the stream. Amy, who rose early to learn her lessons, trips along gathering a nosegay for her teacher.

Six chapters trace small trials of temper and pride: a new leaf to be filled, another attempt after failure, and truth that sets free. Amy learns that scolding and misunderstanding sting most when pride feeds them, and that lowliness eases the hurt. The heavenly seed and dew of the subtitle stand for the good teaching meant to grow in young hearts.
2641-a-room-with-a-view:
E. M. Forster sets this beloved novel in Florence and England, opening at the Bertolini pension, where Lucy Honeychurch longs for a room with a view. In Santa Croce without a Baedeker, among violets, music, and a letter marked S, she meets the Emersons, father and son.

Back in England, Charlotte Bartlett, Cecil Vyse, and the conventions of Sawston press Lucy toward a proper marriage. Forster writes with wit and tenderness about choosing life over manners. The novel endures as a comedy of awakening, and one of the sunniest books about breaking free.
27230-the-voyage-of-the-first-hessian-ar:
The Voyage of the First Hessian Army from Portsmouth to New York, 1776, translated from the German of A. Pfister, appears as Heartman's Historical Series number 3, printed in 110 copies in 1915. Pfister's sketch, published fifty years earlier in a German periodical, adds little-known details of the voyage.

The Hessian divisions had not all assembled at Portsmouth, with General von Mirbach's men still at Bremerlehe for lack of transports. Commander-in-chief Heister refused to sail divided, until General von Schlieffen, the Hessian minister in London, took the matter on himself. An extract from the diary of J. G. Seume, a Hessian soldier on the voyage, closes the sketch.
2770-five-little-peppers-and-how-they-gr:
Margaret Sidney wrote this children's classic for the memory of her mother, wise in counsel, tender in judgment, and strengthful in Christian faith and purpose. The dedication offers the simple book with reverence to that memory.

Five little Peppers in a little brown house make happiness for Mamsie, celebrate her birthday, and endure trouble and hard days, with Polly at their head. Sidney writes with homely warmth about poverty borne cheerfully. The book endures as a beloved story of family love against thin times. Polly's courage holds the little brown house together.
28071-the-red-triangle-being-some-furthe:
Arthur Morrison's The Red Triangle, first published in 1903, collects six further cases of Martin Hewitt, private investigator. Hewitt's friend Brett narrates the tales, which at first seem separate: stolen diamonds, a lever key, a burnt barn, and an Admiralty code. Slowly a single mark, a red triangle, links them to deep, hidden work.

Hewitt warns Brett to wait, sensing more to come behind the first case. The stories move from London rooms to Channel Marsh, with careful deduction rather than chases. Readers of early detective fiction get a neat puzzle: separate crimes that turn out to be one conspiracy.
2869-the-point-of-view:
Henry James wrote The Point of View as a novel in letters, published in London by Macmillan in 1886. Miss Aurora Church writes from a ship to Miss Whiteside in Paris, reporting that her seasickness medicine stayed unopened because she spent the whole voyage walking the deck in animated conversation. Twelve rounds of the deck make a mile, by her measure, and she counts her health a wonder.

Other letters give the same scenes from opposite angles, so that American and European manners correct each other. A later writer praises American houses as fresh and clean against musty European interiors, while admitting that much is still imitation. The book charms as an early experiment in viewpoint, where truth arrives only by comparing voices.
30128-where-strongest-tide-winds-blew:
Robert McReynolds sets a romantic adventure in South America, drawn, the dedication says, from the principal incidents in the lives of John B. Stephen and his wife. Chapters run from under the sword of Damocles and days of innocence, through mists of the sea and graves giving up their dead, to the fairest flower of the Cordilleras. Revolution follows, with Viva Generalissimo Pierola, the din of battle, a meeting again with Felicita, and a masque ball at Tiravaya.

Gowdy-Simmons published the Colorado Springs volume in 1907. Its pictures show sounding the depths, the wreck of the Spanish sloop Seville, the earth rocking and reeling, and the home voyage of the Aven through sea dangers. McReynolds, author of Thirty Years on the Frontier, writes a swift, colorful tale of love, war, and the sea.
31253-a-morning-s-walk-from-london-to-ke:
Sir Richard Phillips's 1817 walk from London to Kew is a pedestrian tourist's observations on home scenery, printed in London and sold by John Souter. His preface disclaims high literary ambition: he has not climbed the Andes, Alps, or Apennines, nor described earthquakes, eruptions, chasms, caverns, and cataracts. He has restricted himself to subjects thousands can examine daily after him.

A habitual independent thinker, Phillips ranks nothing higher as a test of truth than what the senses show and what reason infers from it. He doubts his conclusions will please university professors who teach only their predecessors' doctrines. The walk is thus both a ramble and a freethinker's manifesto, grounded in the road to Kew.
31369-nationality-and-race-from-an-anthr:
Arthur Keith's 1919 Robert Boyle Lecture, delivered before the Oxford University Junior Scientific Club on November 17, 1919, was published by Humphrey Milford. It treats nationality and race from an anthropologist's point of view. Keith begins in Boyle's time, when Englishmen first came into close contact with the races and nationalities of the outer world. Small bands elbowed Native peoples from North America's eastern seaboard, while merchants met the peoples of India, the Far East, Africa, and South America.

Boyle himself, born in County Cork in 1627 and dead in London in 1691 at sixty-four, left minute directions for navigators reporting new lands, covering geography, minerals, products, and climate. Keith notes he left out the inhabitants. The lecture uses that omission to open a modern anthropological question: what nationality and race actually mean.
31932-contamination-crew:
Alan E. Nourse's short story Contamination Crew, framed as a file from the Medical Disciplinary Board of Hospital Earth, opens with orders that a creature had to be killed. It asks how one destroys the indestructible. Its documents come from the preliminary hearings in the case of the Profession against Samuel B. Jenkins, physician.

A dispatch from the general survey ship Mercy, in the Vorochislov sector in the year 2341, reports to Lucius Darby at Hospital Earth, as Jenkins anticipates charges from a fellow physician. Readers get a medical science-fiction story told in reports and testimony, where a doctor's duty and a creature's survival collide.
32283-notes-on-a-tour-through-the-wester:
A traveller's journal records a trip through the western counties of New York State in 1829 and 1830, reprinted in 1916 from The Ariel of Philadelphia. The writer starts by steamboat from Bristol, Pennsylvania, to New York City, then continues to Albany and onward through towns, farms, and country roads. He notes lodgings, fares, food, and the look of streets and settlements as he goes.

The entries read like notes from a practical farmer with an eye for land, crops, and daily work. Readers get prices, such as a dollar for bed and supper and two dollars for the Albany boat, alongside remarks on soil, buildings, and local habits. Together, the dated entries give a plain, first-hand picture of western New York just before rail travel changed the region.
32960-the-competitive-nephew:
Montague Glass's Competitive Nephew, published in 1915, collects comic stories of business, family, and the city, by the author of Abe and Mawruss and Potash and Perlmutter. The title story, subtitled a story of business, nepotism, asthma, and even love, tells of a young man who has barely been in a place a year. He marries a relation of his boss and gains three hundred dollars in the bargain. Other stories follow Mr. Zamp and the sorrows of Seiden.

Glass writes in the brisk, slangy voice of New York commercial life, where cousins, bosses, and bargains decide fortunes faster than merit alone. His humor is warm rather than bitter, and his characters, drawn from the garment and business world he knew, feel like people met in an office or a shop. The collection is a lively sample of American comic fiction just before the First World War.
33286-from-bull-run-to-appomattox-a-boy-:
L. W. Hopkins's memoir, copyrighted in 1908, gives a boy's view of the Civil War, from Bull Run to Appomattox, as a trooper in General J. E. B. Stuart's cavalry, Sixth Virginia Regiment. Its first chapter moves from Harper's Ferry to Bull Run, through Loudoun County on the Potomac and memories of John Brown. Hopkins, pictured in an old daguerreotype from 1861 before entering the army, writes as a youth turned soldier.

The book's strength is its young, first-hand voice, full of marches, camps, and battles seen from the ranks. Its tone is plain and vivid, and its account of Stuart's cavalry adds a Confederate boy's view to the war's literature. For readers of Civil War memoirs, it is a lively, honest record of a war lived young.
34924-florence-hanemann-s-dance-revue-ce: Florence Hanemann's Dance Revue is the printed program for a children's dance show held at Central School in Glen Rock, New Jersey, on June 9, 1950. The program lists each number, its music, and the names of the young dancers, from the Dance of the Sugar Plum Fairy to a gypsy dance and a Russian dance. A fuller scene from Hansel and Gretel names the children playing Hansel, Gretel, the parents, the witch, and a row of angels. It is a keepsake of one small-town school concert.
34938-education-how-old-the-new:
James Walsh wrote Education: How Old the New, a study of how many modern ideas in teaching are older than they look. Walsh was dean and professor of the history of medicine, with degrees in medicine and letters. The transcriber notes that quotes and citations stand indented in the text.

Walsh argues from history that the new education of his day repeats methods the middle ages and the ancients knew well. As a historian of medicine and of universities, he had the long view at his command. The book comforts teachers who suspect that each generation's novelty is an old friend in new dress. It also rebukes reformers who know no past. Walsh writes smoothly, with a store of examples from the schools of other centuries.
34977-dutch-and-english-on-the-hudson-a-:
A history of colonial New York by Maud Wilder Goodwin. Yale University Press copyrighted it in 1919. It forms volume seven of the Chronicles of America series. Allen Johnson edited the series as a whole. A painting of lower Broadway in 1650 fronts the book. Fourteen chapters carry the Hudson story to Sir William Johnson.

Geography is the maker of history, the first chapter declares. The Hudson's hundred fifty miles fixed Dutch settlement's course. Hudson's Half Moon slipped into the harbour in September 1609. Patroons, directors, domines, and burghers get chapters in turn. Leisler's rebellion, privateers, and the Zenger trial follow. Negro plots and colonial government close the political arc. Goodwin writes brisk, readable narrative for the series' general audience.
35528-the-secret-of-the-sands-or-the-wat:
Harry Collingwood wrote The Secret of the Sands, a sea tale of the yacht Water Lily and her crew, in an edition dated 1879. His preface takes up the charge that long voyages in very small craft are foolhardy. Much, he grants, depends on the seaman's skill and nerve, and as much on the design and gear of the little ship.

The story opens on a morning after days of boisterous weather, in a November gale from the southwest worse than any in memory. From that storm the Water Lily's crew sail into the secret of the sands. Collingwood, himself a yachtsman, wrote sea tales for boys that old sailors praised for their truth. This is one of his earliest and best.
37621-the-jew:
Linda da Kowalewska translated The Jew from the Polish of Joseph Ignatius Kraszewski. Dodd, Mead and Company published the novel in New York with an 1890 copyright.

The tale opens at Sestri-Ponente, near Genoa, on a warm autumn day in 1860. The only inn in town brims with people, to the host's delight. Chapters trace the education of Jacob and a simple history of love. A voyage on foot, the Sabbath, and the eve of an insurrection follow. Jews in council and nobles in reunion set the political stage. Jacob flees, love of country speaks, and the insurgents close the tale. Kraszewski wrote of Poland's Jews with scope and sympathy.
38277-from-squire-to-squatter-a-tale-of-:
Gordon Stables wrote From Squire to Squatter, a tale of the old land and the new, in an edition from Shaw of London dated 1888. Fireside talk between a father and his boys opens the book at Burley Old Farm.

Archie turns ten tomorrow, and he feels quite old. Soon he will be a man, he tells his father. His father laughs, since a growing son means a graying parent. Archie shakes his head: other boys' fathers may grow old, but his never could. In the corner lies his younger brother, nine years old and frail. The sickly lad dreams in big dark eyes and wishes to be old and wise. Stables sets a tender family against an emigrant tale.
38356-speciation-of-the-wandering-shrew:
James S Findley studies a small mammal in Speciation of the Wandering Shrew, issued by the University of Kansas in 1955. It stands as volume nine, number one, of the Museum of Natural History publications, sixty-eight pages with eighteen figures. The wandering shrew bears the Latin name Sorex vagrans.

Findley's materials run to some 3,465 museum study skins and skulls, grouped by place, age, and sex. His contents move from pelage change and geographic distribution, across the Pacific coastal, inland montane, and Great Basin sections, to the origin of the species group and its relationships. A table of measurements closes it.
38364-in-pastures-new:
George Ade wrote In Pastures New, issued at Toronto in 1906 by the Musson Book Company. Many letters in the book first ran in a syndicate of newspapers in early 1906. More came from letters to the Chicago Record in 1895 and 1898. Victor F Lawson is thanked for use of those letters. Mr Peasley travels with Ade through the tale.

Parts treat London, Paris, Naples, and Cairo in turn. Getting acquainted with the English language leads the London part. A life on the ocean wave and darkest London follow. The passport and the cable code get a chapter of their own. In Paris, French justice in the Dreyfus case is weighed. In Naples, Peasley's vivid impressions rule. Cairo as a stamping ground for Americans and a visit to the Pyramid of Cheops close the part shown here.
38829-garden-craft-old-and-new:
Garden-Craft Old and New, by the late John Sedding, was issued in a new edition in London in 1895, with a memorial notice by Russell and nine plates. Sedding was an architect who made gardens for the houses he built. A preface borrowed in fun from Stevenson opens the book, with Caleb and Joshua bringing grapes from Palestine.

The editor jokes that Sedding offers accounts of what a fine garden should be, rather than figured plans. The work began as a talk on the craft of gardening to the Art-Workers' Guild, then loosened at home into a gardener's open letter. Sedding argues for gardens as true art, joined to the house in style and spirit, in the Arts and Crafts taste of his day.
39554-the-house-that-grew:
The House That Grew, a story for young readers by Mrs Molesworth, was issued at London and New York by Macmillan in 1900. Pictures by Alice Woodward go with the tale. Molesworth had written Carrots and The Cuckoo Clock before it. A front scene shows a boy named Rolf setting down a little creature with care.

The first chapter opens on a cry that something is dreadful. Muffins for one thing are hoped for in the second chapter. A wonderful idea strikes a girl named Ida in the third. A boy called Geordie stands up and waves his cap in the fourth. What can she mean, asks the fifth chapter head in its turn. Molesworth writes of children, change, and a house that answers to their growth.
40688-the-school-friends-or-nothing-new:
Kingston wrote The School Friends, a boys' tale printed in London by Routledge. Its two heroes, Lance Loughton and Emery Dulman, are schoolfellows at Elmerston Grammar School, both in the sixth form. Lance stands near the head of the form, while Emery sits at the bottom.

Lance is steady, studious, and brave, ever ready to shield a small boy from a bully. Emery, a tradesman's son with big dreams of the army, holds himself the equal of any boy in school. Their friendship, tested by pride, scrapes, and schoolboy honor, drives the tale. Kingston wrote many such books, and this one shows his blend of school life, moral tests, and adventure.
40811-expositor-s-bible-the-gospel-of-ma:
The Gospel of St. Matthew is a volume of the Expositor's Bible by John Monro Gibson, printed at Toronto in 1890. Nicoll edited the series. Gibson also wrote The Ages Before Moses and The Mosaic Era. A note at the front says an advertisement for the series was moved to the end of the book.

Gibson reads Matthew chapter by chapter. He begins with the coming of the Christ, then his reception, herald, baptism, and temptation. The Galilean ministry follows, with the Sermon on the Mount given full treatment. Beatitudes, the moral law, and duties to the world each get their place. The commentary speaks to readers who preach or teach from the Gospel.
43971-one-man-s-view:
One Man's View is a novel by Leonard Merrick, with a famous introduction. Granville Barker, the playwright, wrote that introduction for this edition. Hodder and Stoughton issued it in London, New York, and Toronto in 1922. Chapter one opens on Heriot passing a big pink house in idleness. A girl on the balcony has caught his unwilling interest there.

The idea of seeking her was foreign to his temperament, he reflects. He had noticed her on the terrace by the band stand one morning. A delicious complexion and grey eyes, darkly fringed, drew his gaze. He had unconsciously given her traits she was probably a stranger to. Merrick's irony traces a man's self deception in love's first days.
44286-if-youth-but-knew:
If Youth But Knew, a novel by Agnes and Egerton Castle, was published by Macmillan in 1906. Pictures by Lancelot Speed illustrate the romance. Its motto is the old French song: if youth but knew, if age but could. A front plate shows a child’s eyes asking something yet of a man.

At the touch of his lips, the caption says, Sidonia’s woman’s soul was born. He kissed her gently, as he would have kissed a child, it adds. The Castles wrote bright historical romances as a husband and wife team. Rose of the World and French Nan stand in their list of earlier books. Youth, age, and a love across the gap give this tale its ache. Their novels sold elegance, wit, and a tender moral.
44914-bow-wow-and-mew-mew:
Georgiana M Craik wrote Bow-Wow and Mew-Mew, a tale for young children, here edited by Joseph C Sindelar. The edition is dated nineteen fourteen. Bow-Wow is a dog and Mew-Mew a cat, thrown together in one home.

At first the two are not happy, and Bow-Wow gets hurt and must stay in bed. Mew-Mew turns nurse, and the pair grow great friends. Then they run away together, through fields and a corn-field, and meet a big sheep-dog. Bow-Wow is badly hurt again, and Puss tends him once more. Kind friends and thoughts of home end their outing.
45502-how-the-other-half-lives-studies-a:
Jacob Riis wrote this study of the tenements of New York, published by Scribner in 1890. Most of the illustrations come from photographs taken by Riis himself, the title page states. Gotham Court, a notorious block, is pictured at the front of the first edition.

Every man's experience ought to be worth something to his community, Riis argues in the preface. That belief made him begin the book, gathering his years as a newspaper police reporter. Health board men and Chief Inspector Byrnes helped him finish, he thanks them, in a book that showed comfortable New York the rooms its other half lived in.
48164-the-boy-scouts-of-the-life-saving-:
The Boy Scouts of the Life Saving Crew is a boys' adventure novel by Scout Master Robert Shaler. It was published in New York by Hurst and Company in 1914. The book is the fourth of ten Sterling Boy Scout titles by the same author, among them books on the signal corps, pioneer camp, and the flying squadron.

The first chapter is titled Out on the Trestle, a hint of danger to come. The series formula is plain from the list and the opening. A troop of Boy Scouts is placed beside a working crew, here the life saving crew that guards the coast. Rescue work gives the boys their stage. The publisher offered every title in the set, bound in cloth, at the same low price, postpaid, a sign of how the series was sold to young readers.
48745-captain-of-the-crew:
Ralph Henry Barbour wrote Captain of the Crew, a school story in an edition from Appleton in New York. A list at the front shows the shelf Barbour had already built, with For Yardley, Winning His Y, The Half-Back, and Forward Pass. A front picture catches a tense cry, a plea to keep a promise, quick.

The crew of the title is a rowing eight, and the captaincy brings honor and strain in equal shares. Barbour was the king of the American school sports tale. His boys train, quarrel, and pull together toward race day. Young readers get clean sport, loyalty to school, and the drama of a seat won or lost by grit.
50201-the-young-oarsmen-of-lakeview:
Captain Ralph Bonehill wrote The Young Oarsmen of Lakeview, a tale of boy rowers. W L Allison Company issued the book in New York in eighteen hundred ninety seven. Jerry Upton and Harry Parker lead its cast of lake lads. The Lakeview Boat Club frames their races, rows, and scrapes.

Jerry has the muscle and Harry the skill, their friends all say. A mile race to the great pine and back opens the gay tale. Mrs Fleming’s runaway horse gives Jerry his first brave hour. A sloop saved and a drowning mate pulled out raise his name. Hermit Island hides a hermit with a secret worth the rowing. Tar and feathers wait for one foe in a dark night attack. The Rockpoint Hotel robbery and a red valise knot the plot. Slocum shows his hand at last and is brought to book in shame.
51961-bill-nye-s-chestnuts-old-and-new:
Bill Nye Chestnuts Old and New is a book of humor by Bill Nye, printed in New York in 1888. Fresh plates come from sketches, photos, and notes by Williams, Opper, and Hopkins. Nye was a famed American funnyman of the press.

The first piece takes on the Shakespeare and Bacon puzzle with care. Nye backs the claim of Bill Shakespeare, and jokes that the time has come for humorists to stand by each other. He grants that Shakespeare wed a woman eight years older at age eighteen, and had three small children in fourteen months. He will not defend the man character, yet he holds the man wrote good pieces. The book packs Nye dry wit on books, folk, and folly of his day.
52362-a-history-of-booksellers-the-old-a:
A History of Booksellers traces the old and new trades of selling books. Henry Curwen wrote the work. Chatto and Windus published it in London. Portraits and illustrations fill the volume. A quote from Carlyle heads the title page. Carlyle prized such a history above ten histories of kings.

The preface is dated November 1873. Curwen admits he cannot trace every firm. He follows the trade's origin and growth first. He then gives fuller treatment to typical English houses. The Longman family receives a chapter. Constable, Cadell, and Black share another. John Murray and William Blackwood follow. The book also shows how great works were equipped and furnished. It concentrates fresh attention on the story of literary struggle.
5310-the-point-of-view:
Elinor Glyn's Point of View opens in the restaurant of the Grand Hotel in Rome, filling up late in May as entertainments lessen. Stella Rawson enters with her uncle and aunt, Canon and Mrs Ebley. The party takes a secluded corner, feeling out of place amid gayer company, though the hotel's drains are known to be beyond question.

Glyn, famous for romantic novels of high society, writes here of manners, reputation, and love among English travellers abroad. The novel offers readers a glimpse of Edwardian Rome through English eyes, where a young woman's point of view slowly becomes the story's centre.
55817-automata-old-and-new:
Conrad William Cooke, an electrical engineer, delivered Automata Old and New as a talk to the Sette of Odd Volumes, a London dining club of bookmen, in November 1891. It was printed for the members as the twenty ninth of their privately issued opuscula, at the Chiswick Press in 1893. Cooke served the society as its officer called the Mechanick.

His subject is self moving figures: the mechanical ducks, writers, and musicians of the eighteenth century, and the new electrical and pneumatic automata of his own day. A dedication page names the club's presidents by their club titles: the Pilgrim, the Art Critic, and the Leech. Such club lectures, half learning and half sport, were a Victorian habit, and the printed pamphlets are now scarce.
56526-how-the-garden-grew:
How the Garden Grew, by Maud Maryon, is a year in a rectory flower garden. Longmans printed the book in London in 1900, with four plates by Gordon Browne. A nursery line serves as motto: Mary, Mary, quite contrary, how does your garden grow?

The book is built as four seasons, winter to autumn, with an index. It is given to his Reverence, the rector of the parish. The narrator took the charge because no one else would. The gardener, she says, could not be accused of taking care of the place. The kitchen garden gave some account of itself under the rector's rule. The flower garden, though, cried desolation aloud. She lists the shame: weak geraniums, starved calceolarias, and scraggy lobelias. What she wants are the tall blue things, the round yellow ones fringed with red, and sweet-Williams.
56572-water-wonders-every-child-should-k:
Water Wonders Every Child Should Know tells the young of water's forms. Jean Thompson wrote it, with shots from the lens of Bentley. Bentley was famed for his shots of snow flakes seen up close. The book came out in New York in the year 1907.

Dew is the first of the forms the book takes up for the child. Hoar frost and the etch of Jack Frost on the pane come next. The riddles and charm of snow fill the long midst of the work. Ice and its birth, and the good rain that ends the run, close the set. A verse on a snow clad tree stands at the gate of the book. The tone is warm and plain, made for a child at a knee.
56750-tarry-thou-till-i-come-or-salathie:
George Croly wrote Tarry Thou Till I Come, or Salathiel, the Wandering Jew, in an illustrated edition from Funk and Wagnalls with twenty full page drawings by Thulstrup. An introductory letter by General Lewis Wallace, the author of Ben-Hur, commends the book. The words of the title are the curse laid on the Jew who mocked Christ on the way to the cross, in the old legend.

Salathiel cannot die, and he walks through eighteen centuries of Jewish and Roman sorrow in Croly's vast romance. Croly, an Irish clergyman and poet, poured learning and fire into the tale. Wallace's praise helped it live into a new century. Readers get a sweeping, solemn romance of the undying witness.
5737-smoke-bellew:
Jack London follows Smoke Bellew, a city man turned Klondike adventurer, through linked stories of the Yukon gold rush. Contents include The Taste of the Meat and The Meat. The Stampede to Squaw Creek, Shorty Dreams, and The Man on the Other Bank follow. The Race for Number Three, The Little Man, and The Town-Site of Tra-Lee appear among others. Smoke learns hunger, cold, dogs, and the harsh code of the trail.

Readers get London at his most elemental: men tested by frost, work, and sudden fortune, with loyalty and grit as the real currency. The stories move from comedy to danger without losing pace, and Shorty, Smoke's companion, gives them warmth. Fans of adventure fiction and the North will find a brisk, muscular collection that shows why London's Yukon tales endure.
61271-the-man-who-flew:
The Man Who Flew, a science fiction story by Charles Cunningham, ran in Worlds of If Science Fiction in November 1962. The blurb states the hook in one line. The man who flew could not exist, but he had committed a foul crime. The tale opens under low grey clouds over a city of the future.

A shining metal thruway mirrors the sombre sky of that morning. A few cars scurry with nerves through the streets below. A man named Keller turns from his office window in a dismal mood. His conscience is bothering him, and it marks his every move. He looks over his humbly furnished office with discontent. The thought comes again that he should change jobs if he wants to eat. Guilt and a flying man drive the plot.
61556-guide-book-to-williamsburg-old-and:
Written by William C. Ewing and printed in Richmond, Virginia, in 1943, the Guide Book to Williamsburg Old and New speaks straight to the visitor. Ewing greets guests, hopes they will stay long enough to love the town, and warns them not to rush. Williamsburg, he says, is not a museum but a living town.

The book first tells the story of old Williamsburg, from its start as Middle Plantation. It then walks readers through the church, the palace, the gardens, and the old streets. Plain tips on pace and order help a visitor see the town as Jefferson and Washington knew it.
61982-the-profession-of-journalism-a-col:
Willard Grosvenor Bleyer, professor of journalism at the University of Wisconsin, edited this set of Atlantic Monthly articles on newspaper editing and publishing. The Atlantic Monthly Press issued it at Boston under a 1918 copyright. His introduction opens with President Wilson's saying that the food of opinion is the news of the day.

Bleyer argues that the daily newspaper is most Americans' sole purveyor of that food, and that public opinion in a democracy is built from it. The contents pair attack and answer: Mencken on newspaper morals, replied to by Ralph Pulitzer. Edward Ross writes on the suppression of important news, and an observer on the problem of the Associated Press, replied to by Melville Stone. Henry Watterson treats the personal equation, Harger the country editor, and Alger sensational journalism and the law. A bibliography and notes on the writers close the volume.
62688-a-guide-descriptive-and-historical:
A guide through the town of Shrewsbury, descriptive and historical, is a local handbook by the Reverend Leighton. The fourth edition, issued at Shrewsbury in 1855, carries sixty one wood engravings. Leighton also wrote a flora of Shropshire, the title page notes. Brief notices of noted objects in the country round the town are mixed into the walk.

Appended lists add to the guide's use. One lists the eminent natives of the town, with pointers to books about their lives. Another lists the birds seen in the neighbourhood. A third names the rarer plants native to the vicinity. The motto on the title page sums up the aim in plain words. The book aspires not to be great, only to be useful.
65544-the-assassination-of-christopher-m:
Samuel Tannenbaum wrote this study, The Assassination of Christopher Marlowe, a new view, copyrighted in 1928 and reprinted in offset in 1962. A line from Hamlet fronts it: murder, though it have no tongue, will speak with most miraculous organ. He dedicates the book to a good friend and fine scholar. The argument opens with the arrest of Thomas Kyd on May 12, 1593.

Kyd, the first of the great Elizabethan dramatic poets, was seized on grave charges: atheism, meddling in dangerous matters of state, and publishing seditious libels. He was tortured on the rack and died untimely. Tannenbaum argues that the arrest had far more important causes, and consequences reaching to Marlowe's death days later, than historians have suspected. The book is a detective brief across three centuries, built from state papers.
66948-the-garnet-story-book-tales-of-che:
Ada M Skinner and Eleanor L Skinner compiled this story book for children, printed by Duffield and Company of New York in 1920. The sisters had edited the Emerald, Topaz, Turquoise, and Pearl story books, a shelf of jewel-named sets. An old English song heads the book, praising a nook and a story book over gold.

The Good-Natured Bear, adapted from Richard H Horne, opens the tales on a Christmas evening at Doctor Littlepump's house. Hans Christian Andersen's Snow-Queen follows in shortened form. Frances Browne gives The Story of Fairyfoot and Merrymind. The King and the Cobbler comes from Gammer Gurton's Historie. Cheer is the watchword, with old tales and new side by side for young readers.
67127-the-origin-tendencies-and-principl:
Victoria Woodhull published The Origin, Tendencies and Principles of Government in New York in 1871. Her own firm, Woodhull, Claflin and Company, issued the volume. The subtitle promises a review of the rise and fall of nations. It gives special thought to the future of the United States.

An introduction defends the book's wide sweep. Woodhull says her age splits knowledge into narrow branches. True growth, she argues, sees each thing as part of the whole. The contents range from God in creation to the Constitution. Two pronunciamentos and a review of the general situation follow. Papers treat the limits and sphere of government. Others take up labor and capital, finance and commerce. A closing paper reads the signs and prophecies of the present age.
67634-report-of-the-sanitary-committee-o:
London's Commissioners of Sewers met at the Guildhall on July 4, 1876, to take up new rules for slaughter-houses. Their health committee reported that day, with the city's medical officer of health in support. The Butchers' Trade Society had fought the draft bye-laws hard.

The report answers each trade complaint in turn and urges the board to stand firm. Slaughter yards in a dense city raised real fears of filth and disease. The medical officer sets out why tight rules on space, drainage, and cleaning were needed. This dry record shows public health law being built, fight by fight, in Victorian London.
68323-celtic-mss-in-relation-to-the-macp:
Celtic Manuscripts in Relation to the Macpherson Fraud is a sharp tract by the author of a past work that called Celticism a myth. It came out at London in the year cut in Roman marks on its title page, the close of the eighteen hundreds. Its head is a wall of quotes set as a charge sheet.

One quote gives a great doctors verdict on a famed set of Scots poems: an imposture then, an imposture still. Others mock the bent and sly falsehoods of Celtic tale, and deny all truth in the stock tales of the Saxon come to Britain. A part of the tract, the word first says, was sent to a Scots paper as a reply in a row over old Scots writs and the deeds of Macpherson.
69071-loved-you-better-than-you-knew:
Loved You Better Than You Knew is a romance novel by Mrs Alex McVeigh Miller, issued as number 59 of the Hart Series. Munro's Sons held the copyright of 1897, and the Arthur Westbrook Company of Cleveland published this edition. The contents list more than thirty chapters of love and trouble. Cupid in the Rain opens the book, followed by One Golden Hour and The Sweet Old Story.

Breakers ahead, a dark secret, and a bunch of roses fill the early chapters. Cinthia's elopement, parted at the altar, and an eternal farewell raise the stakes. A deadly feud and a tragic past darken the middle. The motto verses preserved in the copy tell the pattern: it began with a word and grew with the winds, a prayer for pardon unheard.
69315-in-search-of-fortune-a-tale-of-the:
A boys' adventure tale by Gordon Stables, in a new London edition. John F Shaw published it at Paternoster Row. Stables was a Royal Navy surgeon turned prolific boys' author. The subtitle promises a tale of the old land and the new. A frontispiece shows a boy flying over a gate. John Gilpin's ride was nothing to it, the caption jokes.

Book one sits at Burley Old Farm in England. Archie, a chip of the old block, turns ten tomorrow. A day of adventure and an old castle tower follow. Boys will be boys, one chapter shrugs. The publisher's list in front shows Shaw's uniform series. Hearts of Oak and Exiles of Fortune stand among its neighbours. Emigration to a new land drives Stables's plot onward.
70734-the-skeleton-crew:
The Skeleton Crew, or Wildfire Ned, is a penny tale of adventure issued in London in 1867. It was sold weekly for a penny. Engravings and prize draws helped draw boy readers in. The first chapter opens on a December night more than a hundred years before. Snow lies a foot deep. Moonlight falls on a village near the sea, where only the Black Bull inn still shows a light. A merry party, a strange horseman, and a figure called Rambling Bob start the action.

The publisher's pages crowd with notices. They push sister tales, watches, cricket bats, and even Shetland ponies to be given away. Inside, the story runs on secrets and pursuit. At its center stands the captain of the skeleton crew himself. The tale is a lively sample of the cheap fiction that filled working boys' pockets in Victorian England.
70946-constantinople-old-and-new:
Constantinople Old and New is Dwight's big book on the city, published by Charles Scribner's Sons in New York in 1915. Dwight explains that he once lived in Venice and read Howells's Venetian Life there. He resolved to write a Constantinople life of his own, knowing the city, he thought, just as well. The result outgrew the model. Turkish Constantinople, he found, had been strangely little written for English readers in his generation.

So the book dwells on the commoner aspects of the city as well as its monuments. Dwight makes a point of answering the patronizing Western tone toward the East. He does so by showing the picturesque and admirable side of the place. Portraits and photographs, including Bellini's Sultan Mehmed the Conqueror, illustrate the text. It remains a rich American portrait of the Ottoman capital on the eve of its transformation.
7118-what-maisie-knew:
Henry James opens What Maisie Knew with litigation interminable and complicated, settled on appeal as the divorce court confirmed its judgment on the child's assignment. The father, bespattered from head to foot, had made good his case and was appointed to keep her, though the mother's complexion, immensely remarked in court, may have counted against her. A condition soured his triumph: he must refund his late wife the twenty six hundred pounds she had put down three years before.

That sum was paid on a proved understanding for the child's maintenance, with the father promising to take no further proceedings. The novel that follows sees divorce, custody, and adult selfishness through Maisie's young eyes, as she passes between parents and their lovers. James writes childhood's knowledge with irony, pity, and exquisite care.
73174-old-lamps-for-new:
Lucas wrote Old Lamps for New, a book of short essays and tales issued by Macmillan in New York in 1911. The first piece visits Miss Beam's school, where a blindfold girl is led through a garden by a small boy. From that odd, kind scene the book moves in many brief turns of thought and story.

Named pieces track the painter Vermeer, weigh the worth of a tan, visit a deer park and a windmill, and draw five sharp character sketches. Groups of short bits play the roles of builders, interviewers, and fable makers. A revised Fir Tree and a piece on the letter N add fun. The whole is light, warm, and keen eyed.
73315-when-everybody-knew:
Raymond Spears, who signed himself Raymond S. Spears, wrote When Everybody Knew, a western story that opens in the Many Moons Barroom. It was easy to understand Patient Bob's handling of the bad man, the tale begins. A swaggering monster of a man, with long tangled black hair and sunken caverns for eyes, thunders in on thick-soled boots and surges to the counter. Men between him and his goal spread swiftly right and left.

He growls for a drink and takes a ridiculously little one for so huge a carcass, wriggling as the shot burns, filling again and again. Spears wrote hundreds of outdoor tales. The title hints at the twist.
75970-the-massacre-of-st-bartholomew:
The Massacre of Saint Bartholomew is a history by Henry White, printed by Harper at New York in 1868. A frontispiece after Vasari's Vatican picture shows the massacre in Paris, the slaughter of Coligny and his companions. The work is preceded by a history of the religious wars in the reign of Charles the Ninth.

White's preface states his design. He has tried to describe the great struggle that devastated France in the latter half of the sixteenth century. It culminated in the memorable tragedy of Saint Bartholomew's Day. The struggle cannot be understood, he holds, without the condition of the Protestants under Francis the First and his two successors. In those fiery times the Huguenot character was formed. The nation split into two parties so hostile that the extermination of the weaker seemed the only road back to unity. White writes a Protestant history with a steady, sombre hand.
77755-the-wandering-jew:
Moncure Daniel Conway wrote The Wandering Jew, printed in New York in 1881. Conway was known for Demonology and Devil-Lore. His preface owns that no treatise on the subject existed in English, and that foreign pamphlets had slighted the legend's roots in eastern, Hebrew, and Christian myth.

The Wandering Jew, doomed to walk till the end for mocking Christ on the road to the cross, is his theme. Conway treats the tale not as a curiosity but as a mirror of the folk heart, with sad music of its own. Poems and romances the legend bred get their place. Students of folklore get a rich, humane study.
78072-preview:
Preview is a short fantastic tale by Frank Belknap Long, presented as a warning to moviegoers who let their imaginations wander beyond the screen. A producer named Scanlon holds a preview of his new Western for drama critics, for reasons nobody knows. Before the lights go down he lectures them on the experience they are about to have.

Scanlon promises a sixth-sense heightening of perception, a blotting out of the familiar and the substitution of the totally unexpected. His leading lady, Stella, is a stripped actress: no powder, no cream, no lipstick, since makeup would be false to her period. On screen, Robert Mitchum rides into the Black Hills, and new sound techniques make rifles crack from every corner of the theatre. The critics, at first fastidious, begin scribbling in earnest. The tale hints that the preview's realism may not stop at the screen.
78073-the-winner-and-new:
Ib Melchior, a television director, wrote the science fiction story The Winner and New for a magazine of science fantasy. The editor's note calls it his second story for the magazine and praises its odd slant. The tale opens on Quizz Night at the Capitol Coliseum, where host Bob May greets a huge hall crowd and viewers at home.

More than a hundred million sets, the story says, are tuned to the big question contest. The young contestants seem to know far more than they should, and Mars sits behind their strange knowledge. Melchior turns a quiz show into a first contact tale with a sting.
78370-germantown-old-and-new:
Edwin Jellett wrote Germantown Old and New, a sketch of the rare and notable plants of Germantown, Pennsylvania, printed there in 1904. The Germantown Horticultural Society asked for the paper, and Jellett read it at a public meeting on May 9, 1904. It then ran in the local Independent-Gazette.

Jellett gathered his sketch in one hurried week and thought it would never reach book form. He walks the old town's gardens and lanes, naming fine trees and old plantings, lane by lane. Germantown, founded by German settlers in 1683, was rich in gardens. The book is a loving local record, made for neighbors who wanted their green heritage set down before it vanished.
79096-diana-carew:
Diana Carew, by Mrs Forrester, was published in 1900. Lippincott issued the novel at Philadelphia that year. Dolores and Fair Women stand among her earlier books. A notice at the front explains the double title. For a Woman's Sake was the name first chosen. The sheets were printed before the title was found taken. Diana Carew was therefore set before it. A motto from a life of a lover heads the title page. Forty six chapters make the contents. Most are headed Diana's Story, told in her own person. Chapters fourteen to sixteen break the pattern: not told by Diana. The breaks recur at set points through the book. Chapter one gives Diana her entrance line.

Here comes Diana of the Ephesians, her brother cries.
8040-the-bible-king-james-version-book-4:
Matthew's Gospel opens with a genealogy from Abraham through David to Jesus, presenting him as the promised king of Israel. The narrative follows his birth, baptism, and teaching, including the Sermon on the Mount, his parables of the kingdom, his miracles, and his conflicts with religious leaders. It closes with his crucifixion, resurrection, and the commission to make disciples of all nations.

Matthew writes for readers who know the Old Testament, showing at each step how Jesus fulfils prophecy. His Gospel is the most quoted in the church's teaching, and its Lord's Prayer and beatitudes are known far beyond it. In the King James Version, its ordered, teaching style makes it the natural first Gospel for new readers.
8267-the-world-english-bible-web-matthew:
Matthew opens the New Testament with Jesus traced back through Abraham and David, presenting him as the promised king of Israel. The Gospel tells of his birth, his baptism, and his teaching, including the Sermon on the Mount, where he blesses the poor in spirit and sets out a demanding ethic of mercy. Parables about seeds, treasure, and judgment carry much of the teaching.

Miracles, clashes with religious leaders, and the final week in Jerusalem build toward the crucifixion and the report of the empty tomb. Matthew alone preserves the visit of the wise men and the Great Commission to carry the message to all nations. For readers new to the Gospels, it is the most Jewish in flavor and the most orderly in shape.
8828-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
Weymouth's Matthew, third edition 1913, begins with the genealogy of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham, running from Abraham through Isaac. Jacob, Judah and his brothers, Judah by Tamar, Perez and Zerah, on through Hezron, Ram, Amminadab, Nahshon, and Salmon. Salmon by Rahab fathers Boaz, Boaz by Ruth fathers Obed, Obed fathers Jesse, and Jesse fathers David the king, whose line through Solomon carries the list forward.

From that Jewish frame, Matthew's gospel unfolds: birth, baptism, Sermon on the Mount, parables of the kingdom, miracles, and Passion, all in Weymouth's clear modern English. The translation favours plain sense over King James music, which helps a reader follow Matthew's careful structure and Old Testament echoes. This single-book volume is a good first Matthew, complete and readable, for study or for reading the first gospel straight through.
9313-old-greek-folk-stories-told-anew:
Josephine Preston Peabody retold old Greek folk stories in 1897, as a complement to Hawthorne's Wonder-Book and Tanglewood Tales. Hawthorne had told a dozen myths familiar to American children, yet many myths still appealed to readers of ancient and modern letters. Peabody's group fills out that list, with brief allusions to Hawthorne's tales.

An index aids the whole series, so young readers can trace each story. Her retellings are clear, graceful, and faithful to the myths' spirit. The book remains a beloved companion to Hawthorne, opening Greek wonder to a new generation of children.
a-room-with-a-view: E. M. Forster's 1908 novel: Lucy Honeychurch, Italy, and the room with a view. Charming, witty, and quietly revolutionary, it is his most beloved book. The Edwardian classic of love and freedom. Forster's Italy changes everyone it touches.
andreas-the-legend-of-st-andrew: Robert Kilburn Root translates Andreas, the legend of St. Andrew, from the Old English, in Yale Studies in English edited by Albert Cook. The poem tells how Andrew sailed to rescue Matthew from cannibals, facing sea, storm, and heathen foes. Root's version opens a great Old English poem to modern readers in clear verse.
britannica-1911-aagesen-andrew:
Andrew Aagesen receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, signed by Robert Nisbet Bain. Aagesen, a Danish jurist, broke his law studies at Copenhagen in 1848 to lead a reserve battalion in the first Schleswig war. Chairs and codes, not battles, made his name.

Copenhagen made him professor of jurisprudence in 1855, as Hall's successor in Roman law. His digs into the sources reset that field, pupils recalled, and his manner won wide affection. Sea and trade law bear his hand: the navigation law of 1882 is mainly his work. He sat in the Landsthing from 1879, the year of his death. Danish titles of his books fill the close, with Bricka's lexicon as the guide.
britannica-1911-barrie-james-matthew:
James Matthew Barrie (1860– ), a British novelist and playwright born at Kirriemuir in Forfarshire, is the subject of a long 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. Educated at Dumfries Academy and Edinburgh University, he reached writing through journalism, working on the Nottingham Journal from 1883 and then for London and Scots papers. His Scots village sketches, the Auld Licht Idylls, turned his home village into the fictional “Thrums.”

Fiction and drama share the rest of the entry. A Window in Thrums, The Little Minister, Margaret Ogilvy, and Sentimental Tommy show his humour, pathos, and feeling for child life. The Little White Bird in 1902 held the first Peter Pan episode, which later grew into the famous play. Stage works from Walker, London to the dramatized Little Minister are also traced, showing Barrie moving steadily from sketches and novels toward the theatre.
britannica-1911-baxter-andrew:
Andrew Baxter (1686–1750), a Scottish metaphysician born in Aberdeen, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Educated at King's College, he kept himself by tutoring the sons of noblemen. From 1741 to 1747 he lived abroad with Lord Blantyre and Mr Hay of Drummelzier at Utrecht, travelling in Flanders, France, and Germany. At Spa he met the young John Wilkes and made a lasting friend of him. He came home to live at Whittingehame, near Edinburgh, where he died.

One claim fills his chief work. An Inquiry into the Nature of the Human Soul argues that matter has one core trait: inactivity, an inability to move itself. All motion in matter must come from a power outside it, namely God. The body's motions come from the soul, which, being immaterial, is immortal. The book attacked Toland, Locke, and Berkeley.
britannica-1911-bell-andrew:
Andrew Bell (1753–1832) was a British clergyman and school reformer born at St Andrews. After graduating there he tutored in Virginia, took orders, and sailed for India in 1787, holding eight army chaplaincies at once. At the Madras male orphan asylum, short of teachers, he set pupils to teach each other.

The plan worked so well that Bell preached its use everywhere, setting it out in a pamphlet of 1797. Joseph Lancaster spread the “monitorial” method in Southwark, and church schools soon copied it across England. Bell later founded the Madras College at St Andrews and left large sums to Scottish cities for schooling when he died.
britannica-1911-boorde-andrew:
Andrew Boorde (about 1490–1549) was an English doctor and writer whose restless life crossed monk's cell, bishop's staff, and spy work. Born at Boorde's Hill in Sussex and schooled at Oxford, he joined the Carthusian order under age. Dispensed in 1521 to act as suffragan bishop of Chichester, he never filled the post, and in 1529 he was freed from his vows, unable to bear the order's rigour.

He studied medicine abroad, attended the duke of Norfolk, and visited universities at Orleans, Poitiers, Toulouse, Montpellier, and Wittenberg, watching surgery at Rome and making pilgrimage to Compostella. Back at the London Charterhouse he felt himself in thraldom, and Cromwell freed him in 1536. Cromwell then sent him abroad to sound out foreign feeling toward Henry VIII, and his lively letters home close the entry's opening account.
britannica-1911-chinchew:
Chinchew, or Chinchu, is the name usually given on English charts to an ancient and famous port of China in the province of Fu-kien. Its Chinese name is Ch'üanchow-fu, and it stands at 24 degrees 57 minutes north and 118 degrees 35 minutes east. Walls run seven or eight miles around it, though they enclose much vacant ground. Chief exports are tea, sugar, tobacco, china-ware and nankeens.

Remains of a fine mosque, founded by Arab traders who came here, mark its old foreign trade. In the middle ages it was the great port of western trade with China, known as Zaitun or Zayton to Arabs and Europeans alike. Marco Polo, Ibn Batuta and other travellers used that name for it. Sand banks have since choked its harbour, and Amoy has supplanted it, its trade passing through Nganhai.
britannica-1911-combe-andrew:
Andrew Combe (1797-1847) was a Scottish physiologist born in Edinburgh. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica presents him as younger brother of George Combe. Paris study led him to test phrenology on body structure grounds. Skill in brain dissection let him aid his brother lectures with live proof.

Lung disease forced him to seek health in France and Italy. He still built a practice in Edinburgh from 1823 onward. Books on mental disorder and on health laws won wide favor in print. In 1836 he became doctor to King Leopold of Belgium for a time. Climate drove him home, and his last work treated care of infants.
britannica-1911-crew: Crew is a short word entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names a band of men joined for one set task or piece of work. The word is most at home at sea, where it names all who man a ship. The captain stands apart from the crew in that strict use. Some uses leave the officers out of the count as well. The root of the word is traced to an old French term for growth or fresh force.
britannica-1911-decker-sir-matthew:
Sir Matthew Decker (1679–1749) was an English merchant and writer on trade, and a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives his honours. He was born in Amsterdam in 1679 and came to London in 1702. There he set himself up as a merchant. He was markedly successful in business, gaining great wealth.

Honours came to Decker in number during his career. He was a director of the East India Company. He sat in parliament for four years as member for Bishops Castle. In 1729 he served as high sheriff of Surrey. George the First made him a baronet in 1716. His fame as a writer rests on two tracts on trade. The first dealt with the high duties that weighed on the nation and on trade.
britannica-1911-findlater-andrew:
Andrew Findlater, a Scottish editor who lived from 1810 to 1885, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born near Aberdour in Aberdeenshire, he was the son of a small farmer. He studied at night after farm work to win a place at Aberdeen University. After his degree he took divinity classes with the church in mind.

The article turns in 1853 to his link with the publishing firm of Chambers, which shaped the rest of his life. He first edited a revised work for general readers, issued in 1857. His skill marked him out as editor for a planned Chambers encyclopaedia, and he gave that work its character. He wrote many of its chief articles himself and later edited a revised edition.
britannica-1911-flinders-matthew:
Matthew Flinders, an English navigator and explorer, was born in Lincolnshire in seventeen seventy four. He was meant at first to follow his father's work as a surgeon. A thirst for a life of adventure drove him into the royal navy instead. He entered the navy in October seventeen eighty nine as a young man. After voyages to the Friendly Islands and the West Indies, he served in battle.

In seventeen ninety five Flinders went out to New South Wales as a midshipman. For years he set himself to lay down the outline of the Australian coast. He did that work so well that little was left for those who followed. With his friend George Bass he explored rivers and coast south of Port Jackson. The two men used a boat only eight feet long for one bold trip. Flinders later surveyed the islands north of Tasmania in his work.
britannica-1911-forman-andrew:
Andrew Forman (about 1465-1521) was a Scottish churchman, as this 1911 Britannica article recounts. Educated at the university of St Andrews, he entered the service of King James IV about 1489. He soon won the king's favour and was sent on weighty missions to the English, French, and papal courts.

In 1501 Forman became bishop of Moray, and later Louis XII of France had him made archbishop of Bourges. Pope Leo X then named him to the vacant archbishopric of St Andrews and made him papal legate in Scotland. Rivals blocked his taking of the see for a time, but in the end he gained it and the primacy of Scotland. The article quotes Andrew Lang calling him the Wolsey of Scotland, and he died in March 1521.
britannica-1911-fuller-andrew:
Fuller, Andrew (1754–1815), an English Baptist divine, was born at Wicken in Cambridgeshire on the 6th of February 1754. He became pastor of the Baptist church at Soham in 1775 and removed to Kettering in 1782. His book The Gospel worthy of all Acceptation opposed the hyper-Calvinism then common among the Particular Baptists.

When the Baptist Missionary Society was formed at Kettering in 1792, Fuller became its first secretary, and he held the post until his death on the 7th of May 1815. He had by then served the Kettering church as pastor for more than thirty years.
britannica-1911-gough-john-bartholomew:
John Bartholomew Gough is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Gough was an American temperance orator, born in Kent, England, in 1817. His mother, a schoolmistress, educated him at home. At twelve he was sent to the United States to seek his fortune.

He lived two years with family friends on a farm in western New York. Then he entered a book-bindery in New York City to learn the trade. His mother joined him there in 1833, but she died two years later. Grief threw him among dissolute companions, and he became a confirmed drunkard. He lost his position and sank to singing ballads in cheap theatres. The entry tells the fall that made his later platform career possible. A drunkard who had lived the ruin of drink could warn others with a force no mere lecturer could match.
britannica-1911-hale-sir-matthew:
Sir Matthew Hale is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of an English judge. He was lord chief justice of England in his day. He was born in 1609 at Alderley in Gloucestershire. He died in 1676, the heading notes. His father was a retired barrister with a small estate. His grandfather was a rich clothier of Wotton-under-Edge. His mother's kin were the noble Poyntzes of Acton.

Hale was left an orphan at the age of five. A Puritan vicar of Wotton raised him till sixteen. He then entered Magdalen Hall at Oxford. At first he studied with holy orders in view. A company of strolling players turned his head. He cast off study and plunged into gay society. He soon chose a new path for his life. He resolved to serve as a soldier in the Low Countries. Events at home kept that plan from taking hold.
britannica-1911-march-francis-andrew:
Francis Andrew March, an American scholar of language who was born in 1825, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Millbury in Massachusetts in October 1825. He took his degree at Amherst in 1845, where Noah Webster turned his mind to the study of Anglo-Saxon. He taught in schools in three states in the years that came next.

In 1855 he joined Lafayette College as a tutor. In 1857 he took the first chair of its kind, in English language and comparative word study. He taught as well law, botany, and the science of wealth at times. At Lafayette he set up the first strict science-based study of English in an American college. In 1870 he brought out a comparative grammar of Anglo-Saxon and a reader of the tongue. He became professor emeritus in 1907.
britannica-1911-merian-matthew:
Matthew Merian (1593-1650) was a Swiss engraver born in Basel. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces a family that won Basel burgher rights in 1553. Art skill sent him young to Dietrich Meyer in Zürich for training. Work in Nancy, Paris, and the Low Countries honed his copper craft.

Marriage into the De Bry firm took him to Frankfort book trade. After Bry death he ran that press house from 1624 on. His Topographia tomes pictured lands with plates he cut himself in bulk.
