Text by Martin Zeiller joined those views across thirty parts in all. Town views of lasting worth remain his best claim to fame.
britannica-1911-millar-andrew:
Andrew Millar, a British publisher who lived from 1707 to 1768, is the subject of a short life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. About 1729 he set up as a bookseller and publisher in the Strand, London. His own judgment in books was small, the entry says frankly. He made up for it by hiring a fine staff of literary advisers.

Millar did not flinch at paying large sums for good work, then thought very high. Doctor Johnson said he respected Millar for raising the price of literature. He paid Thomson for The Seasons, and Fielding large sums for Tom Jones and Amelia. He was one of the group of booksellers who financed Johnson's Dictionary. The work of seeing that great book through the press fell mainly on him. He also published the histories of Robertson and Hume.
britannica-1911-parker-matthew:
Matthew Parker, archbishop of Canterbury who lived from 1504 to 1575, is the subject of a long life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the eldest son of William Parker, a citizen of Norwich, where he was born in August 1504. His father died about 1516, and his mother wed again. Matthew went in 1522 to Corpus Christi College at Cambridge.

He took his degree in 1525 and orders in 1527, and he was made a fellow of his college that same year. Wolsey sought him for a new college at Oxford, but Parker, like Cranmer, said no. He had fallen in with the Cambridge reformers. When Anne Boleyn was known as queen, he became her chaplain. Through her he gained the deanery of Stoke by Clare in 1535. In 1537 he was made chaplain to Henry the Eighth.
britannica-1911-perne-andrew:
Andrew Perne, vice chancellor of Cambridge University and dean of Ely, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in about 1519, a son of John Perne of East Bilney in Norfolk. At St John College in Cambridge he took his first degree in 1539. He became a fellow of Queens in 1540 and its vice president in 1551.

Five times he served as vice chancellor of the university. His fame rests less on those posts than on his gift for shifting with the times. Like the vicar of Bray, he stayed true to the faith of the nation, no matter what it was. In April 1547 he backed Catholic teaching, then recanted two months later. Under Edward the Sixth his Protestant faith grew firm. When Mary came to the throne, he swung back and gained Peterhouse and Ely.
britannica-1911-pew:
Pew, a fixed seat in a church, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word came through French from a Latin term for a high place or balcony. A pew is usually enclosed, slightly raised, and framed in wood. Its bench ends often carry carved ornament.

Some bench ends show work of the Decorated period, and a few may be older still. They range from plain oak boards to panels cut with tracery or leaf patterns. Many ends bear the finial called a poppy head. The article recalls the great high pews of the seventeen and eighteen hundreds. Those curtained boxes, nicknamed horse-boxes, filled English parish churches for a century. Nearly all have since been cleared away. The church at Whitby in Yorkshire survives as the best unaltered case of that old order.
britannica-1911-pickens-andrew:
Andrew Pickens is the subject of a short life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Pickens was an American soldier in the War of Independence. He was born in Pennsylvania in 1739 and moved with his family to South Carolina as a boy. He rose to lead militia troops in the South.

The article follows his fights at Kettle Creek, Stono Ferry, and Cowpens. At Cowpens he led the front line and twice brought the broken militia back into the fight. Congress gave him a sword for that work. Later he helped take Augusta and fought at Eutaw Springs. After the war he served in state and national lawmaking bodies. He died in 1817.
britannica-1911-plimer-andrew:
Andrew Plimer, an English painter of small portraits born about seventeen sixty three, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of a clock maker at Wellington. He disliked his father trade, so he and his brother Nathaniel joined a band of travellers and roamed with them. In time they reached London.

There he came to the house of the Cosways in seventeen eighty one and was taken on as a studio boy. His skill at painting was soon seen. He was sent to learn drawing, then taken into the main studio till seventeen eighty five. He then set up on his own in Great Maddox Street. His master is said to have called him his heir in art. The entry gives a bright tale of a runaway boy who made his name in fine small work.
britannica-1911-screw:
Screw, the grooved pin of wood or metal, is the topic of a trade and craft entry in the 1911 Britannica. The text first sets out what the word means. A ridge winds round a round core to form the thread. The gap from one turn to the next is called the pitch. A screw cut in a hole, as in a nut, forms the mate to the outer form.

Most of the space goes to shared sizes and how screws are made. In past days each shop cut its own thread, so parts from two shops would not fit. Joseph Whitworth set out a shared plan in eighteen forty one. In some twenty years his plan won out and made fixes far less hard and costly.
britannica-1911-simpson-matthew:
Matthew Simpson, an American Methodist bishop who lived from 1811 to 1884, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Cadiz in Ohio, he studied medicine and began to practise in 1833. That same year he was licensed as a Methodist preacher. He served churches in Pittsburgh and in Pennsylvania towns.

In 1837 Simpson was ordained elder and took a science chair at Allegheny College. A year later he became president of a new university in Indiana. He edited a church paper from 1848 to 1852 and made it a strong voice against drink and slavery. He was elected bishop in May 1852. He was a close and trusted friend of President Lincoln. Lincoln valued his advice a great deal, and Simpson spoke the last words at his grave. His books include a history of a hundred years of Methodism.
britannica-1911-sothern-edward-askew:
Edward Askew Sothern is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Sothern was an English actor, born in Liverpool in 1826. He began as an amateur and turned professional in 1849. For nearly ten years he played in many companies without great success.

His fame came from one small part that he made great. In 1858, in New York, he played Lord Dundreary in Our American Cousin. The part was a caricature of an English nobleman, at first a minor role. Sothern built up its humour until Dundreary became the centre of the play. In London the piece ran for nearly five hundred nights. Dundreary whiskers became the fashion of the day. The entry shows how one actor's comic craft could turn a slight part into a lasting stage legend.
britannica-1911-st-bartholomew:
St Bartholomew, an island in the French West Indies, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is a dependency of Guadeloupe, lying about one hundred and thirty miles to the north-west. The island is shaped like a bent crescent around the bay of St Jean. Its eight square miles are hilly, rising to a limestone hill of about one thousand feet.

The island has no forests, and water often must be brought from St Kitts nearby. Rocks and shallows make its shores hard to approach. Yet sugar, cotton, cocoa, manioc, and tobacco are grown there despite the dry soil. The capital, Gustavia, holds a small but safe harbour. About three thousand people live on the island, chiefly of French descent, yet English-speaking. France held it from 1648, ceded it to Sweden in 1784, and bought it back in 1877.
britannica-1911-tindal-matthew:
Matthew Tindal is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Devon, most likely in 1653, he was the son of a churchman and became known as an English deist. He read law at Oxford and won a fellowship at All Souls College in 1678.

The article tracks his shifts in faith and his bold books. For a time he joined the church of Rome, then came back by 1688. His big book of 1706 backed state power over the church. That book was burned by order of the House of Commons in 1710. His later work of 1730 was held to be the bible of deism. It drew strong replies from church writers for years.
britannica-1911-ward-edward-matthew:
Edward Matthew Ward (1816-1879) was an English painter of history and genre scenes, and this 1911 Britannica entry follows his early career. He was born at Pimlico in London. As a boy he drew clever pictures for his uncles' book, the Rejected Addresses, and designs for papers by Washington Irving. In 1830 he won the silver palette of the Society of Arts.

With help from Wilkie and Chantrey he entered the schools of the Royal Academy in 1835, having shown a portrait there the year before. In 1836 he went to Rome, where in 1838 he won a silver medal for a picture of Cimabue and Giotto. He then turned to fresco painting, which he studied under Cornelius at Munich. In 1843 he sent a Boadicea scene to the contest for decorating the Houses of Parliament.
britannica-1911-webb-matthew:
Matthew Webb, known as Captain Webb, is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Dawley in Shropshire on the eighteenth of January 1848, he was the son of a doctor. He went to sea as a boy and twice saved men from drowning.

The article turns to his fame as a swimmer. In 1875 he swam from Blackwall Pier to Gravesend, a run of twenty miles. That same year he swam the English Channel from Dover to Calais. The feat, done on his second try, made his name. He later gave shows in London and crossed to America. In July 1883 he died in a bid to swim the rapids below Niagara Falls.
by-still-waters-lyrical-poems-old-and-ne:
George William Russell, who signed as A.E., wrote a book of lyric poems old and new. The Dun Emer Press put it out in 1906. Past work fills much of the set. John Lane gave leave for ten poems from Homeward Songs by the Way. Nine more came from The Earth Breath. Macmillan gave leave for seven from The Divine Vision.

A prelude opens the set. Summer Night, Creation, Dusk, Night, Dawn, and Day mark the hours. Dana, Remembrance, and The Hour of the King turn to old gods and kings. Winds of Angus, Natural Magic, and a piece In the Womb fill the heart. Forgiveness, Parting, and A Prayer give the soft notes. Heroes, Blindness, and Brotherhood raise the stakes. Soul dress, earth's twilight, and the parting of ways close the list in the copy held here.
canoe-mates-in-canada-or-three-boys-aflo:
St. George Rathborne wrote a boys' tale of three lads afloat on the Saskatchewan, for the Canoe and Campfire Series. Donohue of Chicago put out the book. A front plate shows a lad at his paddle, near sucked to a whirlpool's maw. Rathborne's kin books line the series page: fur takers, a house boat trip south, and Dixie chums in a motor boat.

Camp mates in Michigan stand fourth in that list. Scout woodcraft on lake and stream forms the stock of the whole line. Each book is pitched, by the series word, as one each Boy Scout should own. Rapids, camps, and game give this book its beats. Three boys, one canoe, and a great north river form its spine, in the plain terms of its title.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartholomew:
Bartholomew, called the Apostle of Armenia, was a Bolognese Dominican born in an unknown year, who died in 1333. A capable theologian and zealous preacher, he was chosen by John XXII to lead a small band of missionaries to Armenia. Consecrated bishop of Maragha, east of Lake Urumiah, he arrived with companions between 1318 and 1320. He learned Armenian, built a monastery for his brethren, and began apostolic labors with their aid.

He converted large numbers of heathens and Mohammedans and brought many schismatic Armenians into Catholic unity. His saintliness and learning spread widely, reaching Armenian monks who sought higher perfection and church unity. He translated the Psalter, Augustine's treatises, and Thomas's Summa contra Gentiles into Armenian, with part of the Summa Theologica. He also wrote original works on casuistry and on the sacraments.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-william-ex: Blessed William Exmew, Carthusian monk and martyr, suffered at Tyburn on 19 June 1535. He studied at Christ's College, Cambridge, became a classical scholar, and entered the London Charterhouse, rising to vicar and then procurator in 1534. Two days after Prior John Houghton was put to death, Exmew and Humphrey Middlemore were denounced to Thomas Cromwell as obstinately resolved to suffer for refusing the royal supremacy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-mayhew:
Edward Mayhew was an English Benedictine who helped save his order's English line, born in 1569 and dead in 1625. From a Wiltshire family long harried for the faith, he entered the English College at Reims in 1583. He studied at Rome. He then worked twelve years on the English mission as a secular priest. In 1607 he was professed by Dom Sigelbert Buckley, the last survivor of the old English congregation.

With Father Robert Sadler, Mayhew thus kept the congregation alive. It joined the Spanish congregation in 1612 and shared Saint Lawrence's monastery at Dieulwart in Lorraine, where Mayhew was prior from 1613 to 1620. He helped join the English and Spanish congregations by the brief of August 1619, and from 1623 until his death he served as vicar to the nuns at Cambrai.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gospel-of-st-:
The Gospel of Saint Matthew is treated first through its canonicity, since the earliest communities read the Old Testament as Scripture and soon gave the Gospels the same authority. A book counted as canonical when the Church took it as apostolic and read it at her assemblies. A Catholic Encyclopedia article traces Matthew's use in primitive tradition to prove that standing.

The first traces are not indubitable, since post-apostolic writers quoted freely and may have drawn on oral tradition rather than a written Gospel. Clement's Epistle to the Corinthians, dated about 95 to 98, holds sayings close to Matthew. Yet it mixes Matthew, Luke, and an unknown source. Ignatius, martyred about 110 to 117, quotes no book literally but borrows expressions and sentences from Matthew.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sir-tobie-mat:
Tobie Matthew, English priest born at Salisbury on 3 October 1577, died at Ghent on 13 October 1655. He was the son of Tobie Matthew, then Dean of Christ Church, Oxford, later Anglican Bishop of Durham and finally Archbishop of York. His mother was Frances, daughter of William Barlow, Anglican Bishop of Chichester. Tobie entered Christ Church in March 1590, took his master's degree in July 1597, and, after harsh treatment from parents angered by his extravagance. He entered Gray's Inn in May 1599, befriending Francis Bacon and becoming member of Parliament for Newport, Cornwall, two years later.

Longing to travel, he left England in November 1604. He reached Florence despite promising his father he would avoid Italy, met Catholics there, and was received into the Church. Returning despite a new persecution, he spent six months in the Fleet prison, unshaken. Allowed to leave, he traveled in Flanders and Spain. He studied for the priesthood at Rome in 1614.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-andrew:
St. Andrew was a martyr of the faith at Lampsacus in Mysia during the persecution of Decius, and this entry tells a story of steadfastness and one tragic fall. Brought with two companions before the proconsul and questioned about their belief, the party saw Nichomachus, presumptuous and over-confident, apostatize under torture. While Andrew and Paul endured the rack and were thrown into prison.

Meanwhile Dionysia, a girl of sixteen who had reproached Nichomachus for his fall, was seized, tortured, and exposed to three libertines, yet protected by an angel. Next morning Andrew and Paul were stoned to death. And Dionysia, escaping to the place of execution and begging to be slain with them, was carried off and killed by the sword Their feast is 15 May.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-bartholome:
St. Bartholomew was one of the Twelve Apostles, mentioned sixth in the three Gospel lists and seventh in the list of Acts. This entry follows a name that tells us both much and little. The name Bartholomaios means son of Talmai, or Tholmai, an ancient Hebrew name borne, for example, by the king of Gessur whose daughter married David. At least it shows Bartholomew was of Hebrew descent.

The name may have been his genuine proper name, or simply added to mark him as Talmai's son. Beyond the instances cited, the name appears nowhere else in the New Testament. Nothing more is known of him for certain. Many scholars, however, identify him with Nathaniel, since Bartholomew never occurs in the Fourth Gospel, while Nathaniel is not mentioned in the synoptics, and Bartholomew's name is coupled with Philip's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-matthew:
Matthew, apostle and evangelist, is examined here through his name, his calling, and his Gospel. The name comes from the Hebrew Mattija, meaning gift of God, and the entry identifies the tax collector called at the custom house with Levi of Mark and Luke. It traces his five New Testament mentions, noting his place among the Twelve and the double-name custom common among Jews.

Much of the piece weighs the Gospel that bears his name: its Hebrew flavour, its use by the early Church, and the question of its original language. It also surveys traditions about his later preaching and martyrdom, separating firm Gospel facts from later legend. The result is a sober reference survey for readers who want the apostle behind the first Gospel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theobald-math:
Ireland's Apostle of Temperance, Theobald Mathew, is the priest whose crusade fills this entry. Born at Thomastown Castle near Cashel on 10 October 1790, he was son of James Mathew and Anne Whyte of Cappaghwhyte. He entered Saint Canice's Academy, Kilkenny, at twelve and spent nearly seven years there, meeting two Capuchins who deeply influenced him. 

Maynooth followed in September 1807, Capuchin profession in Dublin the next year, and priestly ordination by Archbishop Murray on Easter Sunday 1814. Kilkenny held him twelve months, Cork twenty-four years of ministry in the Little Friary, schools, industrial classes, and benefit societies, before his great temperance crusade began. He died at Queenstown on 8 December 1856.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-year-of-jubil:
Year of Jubilee (Hebrew) explains the Bible's fiftieth-year law of release from Leviticus. By Pentateuchal rule, a Jubilee follows seven Sabbatic years, each seventh year of a seven-year cycle. It thus falls after seven times seven years, at the end of forty-nine, as the fiftieth year. Like Pentecost, it follows the cycle's last year, giving two straight fallow years.

The name likely comes from Hebrew for ram, since the year was proclaimed by horn-blowing, though Ezekiel calls it the year of release, hinting at a root meaning to liberate. Leviticus 25 and 27 lay down three acts. The soil rests with no tillage or harvest, though wild produce feeds all for immediate use; sold land returns to its first owner; and Israelite slaves go free. The Jubilee counts absolutely, so a slave from 1930 frees in Jubilee 1950, not 1980.
cordovero-pardes-rimonim-hebrew:
Moses Cordovero of Safed, the teacher of Isaac Luria, wrote Pardes Rimonim, the Orchard of Pomegranates, in 1548. It is the first full system of medieval Kabbalah, gathering the Zohar and the schools before him into one ordered whole. The text here is the Hebrew original, all thirty-two gates, from Hebrew Wikisource. No English version in the public domain exists.

Gate by gate, Cordovero treats the sefirot, the names of God, the letters, the souls of men, and the channels between the worlds. His mind is clear, vast, and patient, a rabbi building a palace for a wild tradition. Luria would rebuild the palace, yet every student still enters by Cordovero's doors.
cuba-old-and-new:
Cuba past and present is the theme of Albert G. Robinson's book of 1915. Fifteen chapters move from old Cuba to new, then round the island. Havana, old and new, gets two chapters of its own near the start.

Sugar has a chapter as the story of the island's wealth. Other chapters treat farm goods, trades, politics, rule, and commerce. The tie with the United States, the wars for freedom, and filibustering all come under review. Photos show Morro Castle, old streets, planter homes, and palm-thatched roofs. Robinson writes for American readers who wanted to know the near island they had helped free. The book is a guide, a history, and a trade survey in one.
dan-merrithew:
A sea novel by Lawrence Perry fills Dan Merrithew, published by the A. L. Burt Company of New York. Copyright was held by A. C. McClurg and Company in 1910, and the book came out on March 12 of that year. J. V. McFall painted four pictures in colour.

Dan meets a girl on the ship Veiled Ladye and seeks the Christmas spirit in early chapters. Then come a lost ship, wits against machine guns, and an attempt on a life. The burning of the Tampico and a night alone on a derelict crowd the middle. Perry thanks Pearson's Magazine, where some of Dan's deeds first ran. The book is swift salt-water adventure of the magazine sort.
doe-osti-2575559-los-alamos-at-30-remark:
Report LA-UR-25-28245, issued August 11, 2025 and edited by Roger A. Meade, preserves a speech from the laboratory's own history. On June 21, 1975, Director Harold Agnew gave the closing remarks at the thirtieth anniversary reunion of Los Alamos. His talk followed Raemer Schreiber's and looked at the laboratory's recent growth rather than its wartime founding.

Agnew traces the numbers with a storyteller's ease. In 1945 nobody quite knew the budget; about 3,000 people worked on the mesa, over half of them soldiers. Ten years later the budget was 37 million dollars with the same headcount, all civilian. By 1965 it was 84 million and 3,900 staff; in 1975, 162 million and 5,300. He notes housing growth and fifty staff with thirty years of service. A national turn closes the account: the Atomic Energy Commission had folded that January, replaced by a new energy agency as an energy crisis loomed.
doe-osti-2588118-hot-cold-or-just-right-:
Ronnen Levinson of Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory was the technical contact for this CRADA final report, LBNL-2001691, dated August 1, 2025. Chun-cheng Piao of Daikin U.S. Corporation was the partner contact, under CRADA number FP00009174. The project challenges a basic habit of building control: thermostats regulate air temperature and simply assume comfort follows.

Instead, the team built a sensor-controller nicknamed Goldilocks. It pairs thermal-infrared and color cameras with machine vision to read occupant skin temperature passively and privately, then closes the loop on heating and cooling around real human comfort. A five-month field study ran in an office building near Houston, Texas. It cut air conditioning load by 42 percent when the room was occupied. The share of comfortable votes rose by 15 percentage points at the same time. The stakes are national: overcooling wastes about half a quad of primary energy a year in United States commercial buildings.
doe-osti-3002353-analyzing-trip-chaining:
Melrose Pan, Hyeonsup Lim, Majbah Uddin, Latif Patwary, and Pankaj Dahal analyze travel habits in Oak Ridge report ORNL/SPR-2025/3955, dated October 2025. The work was prepared for the New York State Department of Transportation. It studies trip chaining: linking errands into one tour, such as work, daycare, and groceries in a single loop. Chaining shapes traffic peaks and transit demand.

The data come from the National Household Travel Survey, comparing the 2009 and 2017 waves for New York State. The team examines who chains trips, for what purposes, and by which modes. A definitions appendix fixes terms such as vehicle trip and worker for consistent counting. Planners use findings like these when they model travel demand and site services. The two survey years let the authors separate lasting habits from one-year noise.
doe-osti-3007111-2025-large-load-literat:
Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's Large Load Literature Review was updated in December 2025 by Vinita Srinivasan and Natalie Mims Frick. It gathers what is known about very large new electricity users such as data centers. It is a living document, revised as new studies appear. A data sources section flags which studies publish their underlying inputs.

More than ninety publications are sorted into twelve themes, from load forecasting and interconnection queues to tariffs, co-location with power plants, and demand flexibility. Each entry links to the source with a short summary of its findings. One theme shows today's large-load forecasts are inconsistent and hard to compare, and it backs shared metrics and a national forecast database.
doe-osti-3018751-high-latitude-low-altit:
Christopher R Wentland, Samantha M Turbeville, Benjamin M Wagman, and Lauren B Wheeler of Sandia ran the climate simulations in SAND2026-16566, printed January 2026. Their topic is stratospheric aerosol injection aimed at high latitudes and low altitudes. The scenario is labeled G6-1.5K-HiLLA, run in the E3SMv3 Earth system model. Control simulations came first. A system identification run then measured how the model responds to injection. From that response, the team designed a feedback controller to steer temperatures toward target.

The optimal aerosol optical depth profile called for 130 teragrams of injection in total. The mass split evenly, 65 teragrams at each of two sites. The authors note the catch themselves: that profile is optimal in a latitude-weighted norm, not necessarily in side effects. High-latitude injection is studied because it might cool the Arctic with less tropical disruption. This overview documents forcing and temperature results for the scenario family.
doe-osti-3023348-truchas-overview:
Zechariah Jibben of Los Alamos National Laboratory gives a short overview of Truchas and its sister code Truchas-PBF, filed as LA-UR-26-22034 in March 2026. Both are open source programs for part-scale modeling of manufacturing processes, built to use high-performance computers well. They can be driven from Python, which lets users run and analyze ensembles of simulations automatically, sometimes thousands at once.

Plain Truchas handles complex shapes and a broad physics set: heat transfer, phase change, diffusion, multiphase fluid flow, view-factor radiation, and electric and dielectric heating, with outputs for microstructure models. Past uses include vacuum induction melt casting, glass additive manufacturing, and solidification research at Oak Ridge. The overview explains when such codes beat commercial software.
doe-osti-3408259-development-and-impleme:
Argonne authors Rachel Thomas and Tyler Sumner report a new AI-based tool that helps build and check fast reactor software models. Building such models by hand is slow and error prone. The tool, whose agent is named Maggie in the text, drafts model inputs for staff review.

Maggie runs on large language models hosted inside Argonne, so lab data stays internal. The agent revises inputs when checks flag mistakes. Some error types resisted full fixes, and later work targets those cases. The gain is speed with control: staff still judge each model before use.
five-little-peppers-and-how-they-grew:
Margaret Sidney opens this children's novel in the little brown house where the widow Pepper sews coats and mending to feed her five children. Her husband died when Phronsie, the youngest, was a baby. Ben is the eldest of the flock, Polly the family's driving spirit, and Joel and Davie fill out the brood between them.

The chapter titles trace the family's fortunes through trouble and sunshine. Hard days, a threatened blow, and a cloud over the house give way to new friends, a letter to Jasper, and Christmas bells. Phronsie pays a debt of gratitude, and education ahead ends the list. Sidney's point is plain: the Peppers are poor in everything except the will to make happiness for Mamsie, and the world eventually notices.
from-a-girl-s-point-of-view:
Bell writes witty essays on courtship and social life from a young woman's side. Her first target is the untrained man under thirty-five. She argues that women must finish the training mothers left undone. Other chapters judge men's clothes and men's talk. Husbands, lovers, and bores each get a hearing.

The book sorts men into comic types. The self-made man and the irresistible man appear. So do the dyspeptic and the too-accurate man. Bell also takes up the New Woman and girls' friendships. Her tone is brisk, amused, and unsentimental. The essays belong to the 1890s debate over changing roles. They read as social comedy with a sharp edge.
germany-and-the-germans-from-an-american:
Price Collier, an American writer, published this survey of Germany in 1913, on the eve of the Great War. Chapters run from the cradle of modern Germany and the line from Frederick the Great to Bismarck, through political parties and the press, to Berlin itself. One chapter bears the wry title A Land of Damned Professors. Another takes its name from the army's motto: no army, no Germany.

Collier writes for American readers who wanted to grasp a rising rival. He treats German schools, women, taxes, and the pride that fed friction with Britain and France. His tone is fair but watchful, and his last chapter weighs the sources of envy and hate between nations. The book is a clear record of how an informed American saw Germany just before the storm broke.
gikatilla-shaare-orah-hebrew:
Joseph Gikatilla, a Spanish Kabbalist of the thirteenth century, wrote Sha'are Orah, the Gates of Light, as the classic guide to the ten sefirot. The text here is the Hebrew original, drawn from Hebrew Wikisource. No English version in the public domain exists. Gikatilla had passed from the school of Abraham Abulafia to the theosophy of the Zohar's circle, and this book is his bridge.

Each of the ten gates treats one sefirah, its names, its work, and the prayers that belong to it. Gikatilla sorts the many names of God into their true order, a task every later Kabbalist thanked him for. The introduction teaches how to pray with the gates in mind. The book remains the clearest map of the sefirot ever drawn.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GarrisonJimDavi:
David Mendelsohn interviewed Jim Garrison on May 28, 1989, more than twenty years after the district attorney's famous case. Garrison spoke about the Kennedy assassination and about his book On the Trail of the Assassins. The interview closes with a recommended reading list for those who want to follow the case further.

By 1989 Garrison was an elder of the assassination wars, retelling his investigation for a new audience. His book had renewed interest in his charges against the official account. The interview preserves his late voice on the case that made him known, along with the books he pointed readers toward.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NewYorkDailyNew:
The New York Daily News ran a series called 'Secrets of the CIA,' and this installment profiles Marita Lorenz. Lorenz, the paper says, 'spied on Fidel' Castro. It credits her with an intelligence coup for the CIA inside Cuba. The series packaged intelligence history as newspaper serial, one revelation at a time.

Lorenz's story was told many times, in many venues, across forty years. The Daily News version belongs to the tabloid telling: short scenes, bold claims, a woman at the center of Havana's plots. Readers meeting her here get the outline that later profiles filled in. The installment also shows how the CIA's Cuban operations became popular entertainment while the files behind them stayed closed.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-RepublicofNewAf:
The New Orleans States-Item reported on August 18, 1971, that eleven members of the Republic of New Africa had been arrested in Mississippi. The arrests followed a shootout in which three lawmen were wounded. The headline prints the group's own word for its members: 'Africans.' The Republic of New Africa sought to form a Black nation in the American South.

The raid on the group's Jackson base was one of the era's violent meetings between Black separatists and the law. The article records the arrests and the wounded officers as first reported. It preserves the local paper's framing of an organization most Americans met only through such stories: eleven arrested, three lawmen shot, a republic claimed inside Mississippi.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SmithMatthew_Sm: Matthew Smith's book 'The Second Bullet' is represented here by an excerpt from mainstream publishing. Smith wrote on the Kennedy assassination, and his title names the debate's core dispute: the bullet that struck both Kennedy and Governor Connally. The identification of the excerpt is marked probable rather than certain in the file. Beyond the author, the book, and its subject, the evidence here does not show which chapters the excerpt covers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_dnsa-int: CIA behavior control experiments, the programs that included MKULTRA's drug testing, are the focus of a new scholarly collection noted in this briefing-book page. The Archive has published on these experiments for years, since they remain the classic case of intelligence research abusing human subjects. The evidence supplied here is the title alone, and the collection's contents are not described. The page serves as a signpost: new academic work on the experiments exists, and the Archive's own holdings cover the primary record behind it.
india-old-and-new:
Sir Valentine Chirol wrote India, Old and New, published in London in 1921. He quotes Sir Thomas Munro's hope that Indians would in time govern and protect themselves. Chapters open with the clash of two civilisations and the enduring power of Hinduism. Muslim domination and Company rule follow.

The Mutiny, reforms, and the Great War bring the story to the Reform Bill. Gandhi emerges in a central chapter, with elections and a new Indian parliament after. Chirol weighs economic factors and rocks ahead in his close. The book is a British official's survey of India in change.
john-rutherford-the-white-chief-a-story-:
John Rutherford, the White Chief is a story of adventure in New Zealand, edited by James Drummond. Its front matter lists a portrait of Rutherford drawn in 1828. Kororareka Beach, in the Bay of Islands, is named as a scene of his adventures. The picture list alone shows the book's deep interest in Maori life.

Illustrations show Maori shoulder mats, carved door-lintels, and greenstone axes. Others display the moko, the tattooing on men's faces and women's lips and chins. Weapons, flutes of bone, and stone tools for cutting hair appear as well. The book tells how an English sailor lived among the Maori and came back with their marks and their stories.
old-greek-folk-stories-told-anew:
Josephine Preston Peabody retold Greek folk stories in 1897. The publisher links her book to Hawthorne's myth books. Hawthorne told only a dozen tales in his two volumes. Peabody adds more myths to complete the set. An index covers all three books for easy use.

Peabody opens with man's old friendship with the Earth. Pan, tree spirits, and talking waters fill her world. She says these tales are too good to forget. Her telling suits children meeting Greek myth first. The stories stress wonder, nature, and old human hopes. Her gentle style keeps the old wonder fresh for young readers today.
parisian-points-of-view:
Ludovic Halévy was a French writer best known in English for his novel The Abbé Constantin. Parisian Points of View gathers nine of his short stories, translated by Edith V. B. Matthews and published by Harper and Brothers in 1894. An introduction by Brander Matthews presents Halévy to American readers.

The stories carry titles like "Only a Waltz," "The Dancing-Master," "The Circus Charger," and "The Most Beautiful Woman in Paris." Others follow a ball-dress, an insurgent, a Chinese ambassador, and a ride in an express train. They are light, polished tales of Parisian society, built on small incidents and sharp observation of manners.
podcast-dannyjones-aPOPC244JEw:
Kris Millegan joins Danny Jones to argue that the FBI still hides Jeffrey Epstein's worst secret. The episode title ties that secret to death rites, blackmail, and deep politics. Millegan is a publisher known for books on secret power.

Millegan lays out his claim that dark rites and blackmail files sit at the heart of the Epstein case. He links the case to old agency tricks and hidden groups. Jones asks what can be proved and what rests on faith in the theory. The talk is grim and wide ranging. The library keeps it as an archive record, and listeners judge the claims themselves.
podcast-joerogan-5Xq_ZYB8rew:
Philosopher and podcaster Stefan Molyneux appears on episode 436 of the Joe Rogan Experience, from the show's earlier, rougher years. Molyneux built a large online audience with long talks on liberty, family, and the state. Rogan was still shaping his interview style at the time.

The two work through Molyneux's core claims about freedom, nonviolence, and how children are raised. Rogan tests the ideas with plain questions, and Molyneux answers in his lecture-like flow. The episode stands as a record of the libertarian ideas that moved through early podcasting, argued at full length rather than in slogans.
podcast-joerogan-xtNk_plhnew:
Magician David Blaine recounts his wildest stunts in this Joe Rogan Experience clip, including kissing a king cobra. Blaine is famous for endurance feats and close-up magic that blur into real danger. On Rogan's show he told the stories behind the pain.

Blaine describes having a dislocated shoulder set during a performance and carrying on with the act. He explains why he seeks out feats that scare even him. Rogan, a fan of extreme performers, digs into the mindset that treats pain as art. The clip leaves listeners both awestruck and a little queasy.
podcast-tuckercarlson-2ZpFleCCTew:
Mike Cernovich, the media figure and commentator, sits with Tucker Carlson for a wide conversation. Its announced subjects are the capture of Venezuela's Nicolas Maduro and the murder of Charlie Kirk. The third is battling demons, taken in a spiritual as much as a political sense.

The mix is typical of Carlson's recent programming, where news analysis and spiritual warfare share one table. Cernovich brings his own following and his own history in online political fights. Kirk's killing hangs over the political talk, treated as a sign of the country's condition. The episode records two allies thinking aloud about violence, faith, and power at a moment when their movement feels both ascendant and besieged. Listeners hear the argument as its makers would tell it among friends.
podcast-tuckercarlson-z8pA2TDXtew:
Catherine Austin Fitts joins Tucker Carlson for a sweeping talk on power grids, bankers, secret bases, and extinction events. Fitts, a former housing official turned publisher of the Solari Report, argues that hidden money shapes the modern West. Her claims reach from finance to underground construction.

Fitts lays out her view that trillions moved off the books to build secret infrastructure. She warns that the power grid is a prime target in any great conflict. Carlson asks how ordinary people should prepare for the shocks she foresees. The episode is deep water, a full statement of her system of thought.
sefer-ha-bahir-hebrew:
Sefer ha-Bahir, the Book of Brightness, is the first classic of medieval Kabbalah. It surfaced in the south of France in the twelfth century, cast as the sayings of second-century sages. The text here is the Hebrew original, in some two hundred short sections, from Hebrew Wikisource. No English version in the public domain exists.

The Bahir speaks in parables of kings, trees, wells, and letters, and through them it births the sefirot, the ten powers of God. Souls pass from body to body in its teaching, and the commandments hold cosmic weight. Its riddles fed the Zohar and all Kabbalah after it. Short, dark, and strange, the book is the seed of a thousand years of Jewish mysticism.
short-stories-old-and-new:
C. Alphonso Smith, Poe professor of English at the University of Virginia, chose these twelve tales old and new in 1916. The set opens with Esther from the Old Testament and Ali Baba from the Arabian Nights. Irving's Rip Van Winkle and Poe's Gold-Bug follow in the American line.

Dickens offers A Christmas Carol, Hawthorne The Great Stone Face, and Stevenson Markheim. Maupassant's Necklace, Kipling's Man Who Would Be King, and O. Henry's Gift of the Magi close the set. One compact course in the short tale runs here from ancient scripture to the modern masters of the form.
smoke-bellew:
Smoke Bellew gathers linked tales of Kit Bellew, a San Francisco newspaper man who goes north to the gold country. The contents name The Taste of the Meat, The Meat, The Stampede to Squaw Creek, and Shorty Dreams. Later tales cover the man on the other bank, a race for Number One, and more. Kit's name shifts as he does, from Christopher to Chris to Kit, and at last to Smoke.

The first tale tells how that change began. Kit's friend Gillet Bellamy writes from Paris with tips to fix the Billow, a budding society weekly run by O'Hara. Kit takes the tips down as his own, as Gillet asked. O'Hara hears him out, fires the critic who wrote on music and art, and then traps Kit himself into a post as associate editor.
something-new:
Pelham Grenville Wodehouse opens Something New on a spring morning in London. Sun falls kindly on Piccadilly. A new jauntiness runs through traffic and folk. Bus drivers jest and chauffeurs smile. Policemen whistle at their posts. Clerks and beggars take up the day with fresh vim. At nine sharp, a young man steps out. His door is Number Seven Arundell Street, Leicester Square.

Arundell Street is a true backwater, Wodehouse says. It runs less than forty yards long. Its narrow mouth off the square hides from the crowd. Two hotels fill one side of the small court. They are not of the smart sort. Rooming houses for the poor fill an other side. Those houses are always near to being pulled down. A new hotel is always to take their place. It never does, and they stand on.
the-angel-over-the-right-shoulder-or-the:
An unnamed writer, billed only as the author of Sunny Side, published this new-year tale in 1852. Its title promises an angel over the right shoulder at the start of a fresh year. The story opens in a busy home, where Mrs. James despairs that a woman's work is never done.

A lamp that will not burn sends her back to half an hour of chores she thought finished. Her husband jokes from the floor, where two small boys climb over him at play, and asks if she wishes she had never married. A yes rises to her lips, then dies at the sight of her family. She settles for wishing she could keep the good of her life without its ills.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-40-mat:
Matthew , given here in King James English, opens as the book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham. Verse after verse uses begat to trace a line: Abraham begat Isaac, Isaac begat Jacob, Jacob begat Judas and his brethren.

Judas begat Phares and Zara by Thamar, and the line runs through Booz by Rachab and Obed by Ruth to Jesse. Jesse begat David the king, and David begat Solomon by the wife of Urias. Kings follow, Roboam, Abia, Asa, Josaphat, Joram, and Ozias among them. Family descent, including women and a scandal, frames Jesus before any teaching.
the-nuts-of-knowledge-lyrical-poems-old-:
A.E., the pen name of the Irish poet George Russell, gathered his lyrical poems old and new under the title The Nuts of Knowledge. The Dun Emer Press printed the book, with thanks to John Lane for leave to reprint ten poems from Homeward Songs By The Way and ten from The Earth Breath. A dedication offers the poems to Brian when he is grown up.

The contents list mystical titles: The Hermit, The Divine Vision, The Burning Glass, Aphrodite, Krishna, and A Call of the Sidhe. Poems of earth, breath, and vision sit beside Babylon and Janus. The short list shows a poet blending Irish myth, Eastern faith, and quiet nature worship.
the-point-of-view:
Henry James's The Point of View was published by Macmillan and Co. at London in 1886. It is written as letters. The first comes from Miss Aurora Church, at sea, to Miss Whiteside in Paris. It should not be confused with Elinor Glyn's novel of exactly the same title in the sibling record, a different work entirely.

Aurora reports that the bromide of sodium recommended to her proved useless only because she never needed it. She spent the voyage on deck, walking twelve rounds to the mile and twenty miles a day. She came down to every meal with a fish-wife's appetite. The Atlantic stayed blue and smooth, and land is now in sight before the bay of New York. Her only sharp memories of the earlier voyage are of a severe mother. That mother shut her up daily to learn a religious poem by heart at five.
the-taming-of-the-shrew: William Shakespeare's Taming of the Shrew is the named play of this record, yet the pages present hold only a long editor's note about old printing habits. The note explains exchanged letters such as u for v, blames printers who packed type into cliches, and defends keeping the old errors in the text. Oddly, the note speaks of presenting the First Part of Henry VI rather than the Shrew, a mismatch worth flagging. No scene, character, or line of the comedy itself appears in what is shown.
the-third-and-last-part-of-conny-catchin:
Printed by T. Scarlet for C. Burby in 1592, The Third and Last Part of Conny-Catching, signed only R. G., exposes the sly devices of London's conny-catchers, the con artists of Elizabethan England. Its address promises readers the wonderful, hellish tricks of that crew, plus a newly devised art of fool-taking. The opening reaches back to Henry IV's time, when sturdy, loose companions haunted London waiting for chances to prey on honest citizens.

Against them stands Sir Richard Whittington, the famous thrice-serving Lord Mayor, who drove idle rogues to honest trades or the king's wars. The pamphlet mixes rogue history with warning. Modern readers get a vivid, slangy window into Elizabethan crime, written by an author who presents himself as its sworn exposer.
the-turn-of-the-screw:
Henry James wrote this tale of a governess and two children in 1898. It first ran in a magazine, then came out as a book the same year. James was an American who lived in England, a master of the fine shades of the mind.

A young woman takes charge of two sweet children at a lone great house named Bly. She comes to hold that the ghosts of a past staff pair haunt and mar the young pair. James never tells us if the ghosts are real or in her mind, and that doubt is the tale's fame.
the-world-english-bible-web-matthew:
Matthew, book forty in the World English Bible, opens with a genealogy of Jesus Christ. He is named son of David and son of Abraham. Isaac follows Abraham in the line, and then comes Jacob. Judah's line continues through Perez and Hezron. Boaz appears, born to Rahab in the list. Ruth becomes mother of Obed, Jesse's father.

Jesse then fathers David the king. Solomon follows, born to Uriah's former wife. A footnote explains that Christ and Messiah both mean Anointed One. The genealogy ties Jesus to Israel's whole story. Teaching blocks and parables fill the Gospel after this anchor. Matthew presents Jesus as promised king and teacher.
vital-etz-hayyim-hebrew:
Hayyim Vital, the chief disciple of Isaac Luria, wrote down his master's teaching in the Etz Hayyim, the Tree of Life. Luria taught by word of mouth in Safed and died in 1572; Vital's book is the record the whole Lurianic school rests on. The text here is the Hebrew original, from Hebrew Wikisource. No English version in the public domain exists.

The Etz Hayyim tells how the infinite God drew back to make room for a world. It tells how the light broke its vessels, and how man's prayer gathers the scattered sparks. This myth of breaking and repair remade Judaism and fed Hasidism. Vital guarded the book jealously in his lifetime. Its pages are the fountain of Lurianic Kabbalah.
weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-speech-:
Matthew is book 40 in R. F. Weymouth's modern speech New Testament, third edition, 1913. The Gospel starts not with a birth tale but with a family list. Jesus is named as son of David and son of Abraham. Name follows name through Isaac, Jacob, and Judah.

The list runs past Tamar, Rahab, and Ruth, then on to King David and Solomon. It crosses the exile to Babylon and comes down to Joseph, husband of Mary. Fourteen generations mark each great stretch of the line. Weymouth sets out the names in clean order. Readers see Jesus placed at the end of a long, storied line.
what-maisie-knew:
Henry James opens What Maisie Knew with a long court fight over a small girl. Divorce judges confirm that Maisie Farange will live with her father, Beale. Yet a catch spoils his win: he must repay money his former wife Ida had put down for the child's keep. He cannot raise the sum at all.

A deal then wipes out the debt and splits the child instead. Maisie will spend six months at a time with each parent in turn. James tells the tale through the child's eyes as far as he can. Readers watch adults scheme, charm, and fail around a girl who learns fast. The prose is dense, sly, and close.
